en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.1 (SN 12.1, PTS SN ii 1) 1. Buddhavagga: Discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādasutta) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, it is through dependent origination that this world has become subject to affliction, beset by affliction, overwhelmed by affliction. And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is, from ignorance as a condition there are volitional formations; from volitional formations as a condition, consciousness; from consciousness as a condition, name-and-form; from name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases; from the six sense bases as a condition, contact; from contact as a condition, feeling; from feeling as a condition, craving; from craving as a condition, clinging; from clinging as a condition, existence; from existence as a condition, birth; from birth as a condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called dependent origination. [The Blessed One then repeated the entire formula of dependent origination in forward and reverse order. “This, bhikkhus, is called dependent origination. At these words, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. “Indeed, bhikkhu, it is so. It is wonderful, bhikkhu! It is marvelous, bhikkhu! How well this has been stated by me: ‘When this exists, that comes to be... [The Blessed One then repeated the entire formula of dependent origination in forward and reverse order once more. “This, bhikkhu, is called dependent origination. Then that bhikkhu, having understood the meaning of the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and departed. Not long after that bhikkhu had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu is one who has attained the supreme goal, the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples here in this assembly who are capable of explaining in detail the meaning of what has been stated in brief. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination.
Listen to it and attend closely; I will speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?
With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations [arise].”
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises.
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
This, monks, is called dependent origination.
But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness;
from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.
With the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact;
with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
With the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence.
With the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth;
with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The first [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.2 (SN 12.2, PTS SN ii 2) 1. Buddhavagga Vibhaṅgasutta The Discourse on Analysis At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. "Yes, venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be; whether there is an arising of Tathāgatas or no arising of Tathāgatas, this nature of phenomena stands, this causal status of phenomena stands, namely, 'with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be. ... [and so on with each link] ... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called dependent origination. "And what, bhikkhus, are the dependently arisen phenomena? Aging-and-death, bhikkhus, is dependently arisen, subject to origination, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. ... [and so on with each link] ... Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. These, bhikkhus, are called the dependently arisen phenomena. "Thus, bhikkhus, one who sees dependent origination sees these phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom thus: 'This is suffering'; one who sees dependent origination sees these phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom thus: 'This is the origin of suffering'; one who sees dependent origination sees these phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom thus: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; one who sees dependent origination sees these phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom thus: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. [The Buddha then explains the analysis of each term in detail. "Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has seen this well with correct wisdom thus as it really is, he entirely turns away from aging-and-death, detaches his mind from it, and liberates his mind from it. He entirely turns away from birth... existence... clinging... craving... feeling... contact... the six sense bases... name-and-form... consciousness... mental formations, detaches his mind from them, and liberates his mind from them. When his mind is liberated, he understands: 'It is liberated. He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One's words. (This concludes the first discourse in the Chapter on the Buddhas.)
Staying at Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One said]: “Monks, I will teach you dependent origination; I will analyze it for you.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?”
With ignorance as condition, monks, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises.
With feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises.
With existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

And what, monks, is aging-and-death? That which, for various beings in their respective classes of beings, is aging, decrepitude, brokenness, graying of hair, wrinkling of skin, the decline of the life-span, and the maturation of the faculties—this is called aging. And what is death? That which, for various beings in their respective classes of beings, is the passing away, the perishing, the dissolution, the disappearance, the dying, the completion of time, the breaking up of the aggregates, and the laying down of the body—this is called death.
This, monks, is called aging-and-death.

The passing away, the perishing, the dissolution, the disappearance, the death, the dying, the completion of time, the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the body of this or that being from this or that class of beings—
this is called death. Thus, this aging and this death.
This, monks, is called aging-and-death.
And what, monks, is birth?
It is the birth, the being born, the descent, the manifestation, the appearance of the aggregates, and the acquisition of the sense-bases of this or that being in this or that class of beings.
This, monks, is called birth.
And what, monks, is existence? There are these three existences, monks: [the sense-sphere existence, the fine-material existence, and the immaterial existence].
Sensual existence, fine-material existence, and immaterial existence.
This, monks, is called existence.
And what, monks, is clinging?
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clinging:
clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.
This, bhikkhus, is called clinging.”
And what, monks, is craving?
There are these six classes of craving, monks:
craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
This, monks, is called craving.
And what, monks, is feeling?
There are these six classes of feeling: [the six bases of contact].
Feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
This, monks, is called feeling.
And what, monks, is contact?
“Monks, there are these six classes of contact:
eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
This, monks, is called contact.”
And what, monks, is the sixfold sense base?
The eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base,
and the mind base— this, monks, is called the sixfold sense base.
And what, monks, is name-and-form?
Feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—
this is called name.
The four great elements and the derived matter of the four great elements—
this is called form.
Thus, this is name and this is form.
This, monks, is called name-and-form.
And what, monks, is consciousness?
There are these six classes of consciousness, monks:
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
This, monks, is called consciousness.
And what, monks, are volitional formations?
“Monks, there are three formations:
the bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation.
These, monks, are called formations.”
And what, monks, is ignorance?
It is, monks, not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, and not knowing the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, monks, is called ignorance.
"Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations;
with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness...
Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering."
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
with the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.3 (SN 12.3, PTS SN ii 4) 1.
Buddhavagga
The Discourse on the Way of Practice.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling...
"Monks, I will teach you the wrong way of practice and the right way of practice."
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the wrong way of practice?
With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations [come to be];
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness …” [and so on].
In this way there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
This, monks, is called the wrong way of practice.
And what, monks, is the right way of practice?
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance,
there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations,
there is the cessation of consciousness … [and so on] … such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
“This, monks, is called the right way of practice. This is the third [sutta].

1. The Chapter on Buddhas:
The Discourse on Vipassi.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling... (as before)...
“Bhikkhus, before his enlightenment, while he was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
‘Alas, this world has fallen into trouble; it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn.
Yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from old age and death.’”
‘When indeed will an escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be discerned?
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does aging and death come to be? With what as condition does aging and death arise?’”
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be; aging-and-death has birth as its condition.
Then, monks, this occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does birth come to be? With what as condition does birth arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When existence exists, birth comes to be; with existence as condition, birth arises.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"When what exists does becoming come to be? With what as condition does becoming arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When there is clinging, existence comes to be; with clinging as condition, existence arises.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does clinging come to be? With what as condition does clinging arise?’
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
"When craving exists, clinging comes to be; with craving as condition, there is clinging.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does craving come to be? With what as condition does craving arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī an understanding through insight:
‘When feeling exists, craving comes to be; with feeling as condition, craving arises.’
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"When what exists does feeling come to be? With what as condition does feeling arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom.
‘When there is contact, feeling comes to be; contact is the condition for feeling.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does contact come to be? What is the condition for contact?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
"When the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does the sixfold sense base come to be? With what as condition does the sixfold sense base arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When name-and-form exists, the sixfold sense base comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, the sixfold sense base arises.’”
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"When what exists does name-and-form come to be? With what as condition does name-and-form arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists does consciousness come to be? With what as condition is there consciousness?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When formations exist, consciousness comes to be; consciousness has formations as its condition.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what exists do volitional formations come to be? With what as condition do volitional formations arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī an understanding through higher wisdom:
‘When ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be; with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.’
Thus, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations;
with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness ...
[and so on] ... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
“‘Origination, origination,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, and light arose.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what is absent does aging and death not come to be? By the cessation of what does the cessation of aging and death occur?’”
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
"When birth does not exist, aging and death do not come to be; with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
Then, monks, this occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what does not exist is birth not found? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of birth occur?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassi a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When existence does not exist, birth does not occur; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.’”
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisattva Vipassī:
"What being absent does existence not come to be? From the cessation of what does the cessation of existence occur?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisattva Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When there is no clinging, existence does not come to be; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘In the absence of what does clinging not come to be? With the cessation of what does the cessation of clinging occur?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When craving does not exist, clinging does not come to be; with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging.
Then, monks, this occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what is absent does craving not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of craving occur?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When feeling is absent, craving does not come to be; with the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving.’”
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisattva Vipassī:
"In the absence of what does feeling not come to be? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of feeling?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there came to the Bodhisattva Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When contact does not exist, feeling does not come to be; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘In the absence of what does contact not exist? With the cessation of what is there the cessation of contact?’”
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When the six sense bases do not exist, contact does not come to be; with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what does not exist does the sixfold sense base not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of the sixfold sense base occur?
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When name-and-form does not exist, the sixfold sense base does not come to be; through the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the sixfold sense base.’”
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
"In the absence of what does name-and-form not come to be? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of name-and-form?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
‘When consciousness is absent, name-and-form does not come to be; with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form.
Then, monks, it occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘In the absence of what does consciousness not come to be? With the cessation of what is there the cessation of consciousness?’
Then, monks, through wise attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by means of wisdom:
“When volitional formations do not exist, consciousness does not come to be; with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness.
Then, monks, this occurred to the Bodhisatta Vipassī:
‘When what does not exist do volitional formations not come to be? Through the cessation of what does the cessation of volitional formations occur?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī a breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not come to be; through the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.’
Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
“‘Cessation, cessation,’ monks, regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassi; knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose.
This is the fourth [discourse].
(This should be expanded in the same way for all seven Buddhas.)

Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.5 (SN 12.5, PTS SN ii 9) 1. Buddhavagga Sikhīsutta The Discourse on Sikhī Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there were these four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past. What four? Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, and Koṇāgamana. These, bhikkhus, were the four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past. There will be these four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future. What four? Metteyya, Dhammadassi, Siddhattha, and Tissa. These, bhikkhus, will be the four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future. There were these four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past. What four? Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, and Kakusandha. These, bhikkhus, were the four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past. There will be these four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future. What four? Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, Gotama, and Metteyya. These, bhikkhus, will be the four Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, and Koṇāgamana—these were the Buddhas who appeared in the past. Metteyya, Dhammadassi, Siddhattha, and Tissa—these will be the Buddhas who appear in the future. Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, and Kakusandha—these were the Buddhas who appeared in the past. 1. The Chapter on Buddhas:
The Discourse on the Gotamas “Bhikkhus, before my full enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this occurred to me:”
‘Alas, this world has fallen into trouble; it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and reappears.
Yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death.
When, indeed, will an escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be made known?’”
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? By what condition does aging-and-death arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there came to me the breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be; with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘What being present does birth come to be? …’ [and so on].
existence … clinging … craving …
Feeling … contact … the six sense bases …
‘Name-and-form … consciousness … volitional formations come to be; with what as condition do volitional formations arise?’”
Through careful attention, monks, there arose in me, by means of wisdom, this breakthrough:
"When ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be; with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
And so, in this way, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises...
Thus there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
"Origination, origination"—thus, monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"In the absence of what does aging and death not come to be? Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of aging and death?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there came to me the breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When there is no birth, aging and death do not come to be; with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘What being absent does birth not come to be? …’ [and so on].
existence … clinging … craving …
Feeling … contact … the six sense bases …
‘If name-and-form … consciousness … volitional formations do not exist, through the cessation of what is there the cessation of volitional formations?’”
“Through careful attention, monks, there arose in me, by means of wisdom, this direct realization:
‘When ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not come to be; with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
Thus, indeed, with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.”
“With the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
[as before] ...In this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
‘Cessation, cessation,’ monks, regarding these things unheard of by me before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose.”
The Tenth.

Its summary:

Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.11 (SN 12.11, PTS SN ii 11) 2.
Āhāravagga (The Chapter on Nutriment)
The Discourse on Nutriments.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. …
“Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
What are the four?
Edible food, whether gross or subtle; second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness.”
“Monks, these four nutriments are for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
Monks, what is the source of these four nutriments? What is their origin? From what are they born? From what do they arise?
These four nutriments have craving as their source, craving as their origin; they are born from craving and arise from craving.”
“Monks, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the arising of this craving?
Craving has feeling as its source, feeling as its origin, feeling as its birth, feeling as its arising.
And what, monks, is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the arising of this feeling?”
Feeling has contact as its source, contact as its origin, contact as its birth, and contact as its arising.
And what, monks, is the source of this contact, what is its origin, what is its birth, and what is its arising?
Contact has the six sense bases as its source, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its birth, and the six sense bases as its arising.
“Bhikkhus, what is the source of these six sense bases? What is their origin, what is their birth, what is their arising?
The six sense bases have name-and-form as their source, name-and-form as their origin, name-and-form as their birth, name-and-form as their arising.
And what, bhikkhus, is the source of this name-and-form? What is its origin, what is its birth, what is its arising?”
Name-and-form has consciousness as its source, consciousness as its origin, consciousness as its birth, and consciousness as its arising.
And what, monks, is the source of this consciousness, what is its origin, what is its birth, and what is its arising?
Consciousness has volitional formations as its source, volitional formations as its origin, volitional formations as its birth, and volitional formations as its arising.
“Monks, what is the source of these volitional formations? What is their origin? From what are they born?
From what do they arise? Volitional formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and ignorance as their arising.
Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be.”
With volitional formations as condition,
consciousness arises … and so on … such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
“With the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
The first.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.12 (SN 12.12, PTS SN ii 12) 2. Āhāravagga Moḷiyaphaggunasutta Then the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguno approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Phagguno, one who has not abandoned lust for the nutriment of contact, who has not abandoned desire for it, who has not abandoned craving for it, who has not abandoned passion for it, who has not abandoned fever for it, who has not abandoned thirst for it—he is not freed from birth, aging, and death; he is not freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not freed from suffering, I say. One who has not abandoned lust for the nutriment of volitional formations... for the nutriment of consciousness... for the nutriment of sensory contact... for the nutriment of mental volition, who has not abandoned desire for it, who has not abandoned craving for it, who has not abandoned passion for it, who has not abandoned fever for it, who has not abandoned thirst for it—he is not freed from birth, aging, and death; he is not freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not freed from suffering, I say. But, Phagguno, one who has abandoned lust for the nutriment of contact, who has abandoned desire for it, who has abandoned craving for it, who has abandoned passion for it, who has abandoned fever for it, who has abandoned thirst for it—he is freed from birth, aging, and death; he is freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is freed from suffering, I say. One who has abandoned lust for the nutriment of volitional formations... for the nutriment of consciousness... for the nutriment of sensory contact... for the nutriment of mental volition, who has abandoned desire for it, who has abandoned craving for it, who has abandoned passion for it, who has abandoned fever for it, who has abandoned thirst for it—he is freed from birth, aging, and death; he is freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is freed from suffering, I say. When this was said, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguno said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to point out the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Blessed One—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination. “Phagguno, one who formerly belonged to another sect and desires the going forth and the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline must live on probation for four months. At the end of the four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with him, they may grant him the going forth and the higher ordination to the status of a bhikkhu. However, there are two exceptions: one who has committed a grave offense and a blood-stained murderer. These do not have to live on probation. “I am content, venerable sir, with probation for four days. Let the Blessed One grant me the going forth and the higher ordination. Then the Blessed One granted the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguno the going forth and the higher ordination. And the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguno, not long after his higher ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, here and now entered upon and abided in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguno became one of the arahants.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.

"Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth. What are the four? [The remainder of the discourse follows]"
“Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments: physical food, whether gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; and consciousness is the fourth.
These, bhikkhus, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
When this was said, the Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Who then, venerable sir, consumes the nutriment consciousness?
“This is not a proper question,” the Blessed One said.
“I do not say ‘one consumes.’”
If I were to say, “One feeds,” then this would be a fitting question:
“Who, venerable sir, is it that feeds?
But I do not speak in this way.
If someone were to ask me, who speaks thus:
“Venerable sir, for what is the nutriment of consciousness?”—this is a fitting question.
And herein, this is the fitting answer:

“Consciousness as nutriment is a condition for the production of renewed existence in the future; when that has come to be, there are the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.
“Who, venerable sir, is it that contacts?
“The question is not appropriate,” the Blessed One said.
“I do not say, ‘one touches.
If I were to say, ‘one touches,’ then this would be a fitting question:
‘Who, venerable sir, is it that touches?’”
And so I do not speak thus.
If someone were to ask me, while I am not speaking thus:
"Venerable sir, with what as condition does contact arise?", that would be a proper question.
“In this regard, it is appropriate to explain:
‘With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises.
“But, Bhante, who is it that feels?”
“It is not an appropriate question,” the Blessed One said.
“I do not say ‘it feels.
If I were to say ‘it feels,’ then it would be an appropriate question regarding that:”
“Who, venerable sir, experiences?”—
thus I do not say.
If one were to ask me this while I am not speaking in that way:
“‘With what as condition, venerable sir, is there feeling?’—this is a fitting question.
To this, a fitting answer is:
‘With contact as condition there is feeling; with feeling as condition there is craving.’”
“Who, venerable sir, is it that trembles?
“That is not a fitting question,” the Blessed One said.
“I do not say ‘one who trembles.’”
If I were to say, “It is tormented,” then a proper question would be:
“Venerable sir, who is it that is tormented?
But I do not speak in this way.
If someone were to ask me, who am speaking thus,
"Venerable sir, what is the condition for craving?", that would be a fitting question.
And this would be a fitting answer to it:
“With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises.
“Who, venerable sir, is it that clings?
“That is not a fit question,” the Blessed One said.
“I do not say, ‘one appropriates.
If I were to say, ‘one appropriates,’ then this would be a fitting question:
‘Who, venerable sir, is it that appropriates?’”
And I do not speak thus.
Should anyone ask me, while I am not speaking thus:
“Venerable sir, what is the condition for clinging?”—this would be a proper question.
In this regard, it is fitting to declare:
“With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises” ... [and so on] ...
Thus occurs the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
But, Phagguna, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of the six bases of contact, there is the cessation of contact;
with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
With the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming.
With the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
The Second.

The Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there. “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand aging-and-death, its origin, [its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation]...”

They do not understand aging-and-death; they do not understand the cessation of aging-and-death; they do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death. [They do not understand] birth...
existence... [and so on].
clinging … craving … feeling …
Contact … the six sense bases … name-and-form …

“Bhikkhus, those who do not understand consciousness … who do not understand volitional formations, who do not understand the origin of volitional formations, who do not understand the cessation of volitional formations, and who do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations—
they, bhikkhus, are neither ascetics among ascetics nor brahmins among brahmins.”

They are esteemed as brahmins, yet those venerable ones do not dwell having themselves realized through direct higher knowledge, in this very life, the goal of the ascetic life or the goal of the brahmin life.

But whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, understand aging-and-death, understand the origin of aging-and-death, understand the cessation of aging-and-death, and understand the way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death;
Birth … [and so on] … existence … clinging …
craving … feeling … contact …
The six sense bases … name-and-form … consciousness …

Those who understand volitional formations, understand the origin of volitional formations, understand the cessation of volitional formations, and understand the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations—
these, monks, whether they be ascetics or brahmins, are among ascetics truly accounted as ascetics and among brahmins truly accounted as brahmins;
and these venerable ones, in this very life, have attained the goal of asceticism and the goal of brahminhood.
“Having realized it for myself through direct knowledge, I dwell having attained it.
The third.

2. Āhāravagga, Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand these phenomena, do not understand the origin of these phenomena,

do not understand the cessation of these phenomena, and do not understand the way leading to the cessation of these phenomena— what phenomena do they not understand? Of what phenomena [do they not understand the origin]?”
They do not understand its origin; of which phenomena do they not understand the cessation, and of which phenomena do they not understand the practice leading to their cessation?

They do not understand aging-and-death; they do not understand the origin of aging-and-death; they do not understand the cessation of aging-and-death; they do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death.
Birth … [and so on] … existence … clinging …
craving … feeling … contact …
The six sense bases … name-and-form … consciousness …

They do not understand volitional formations; they do not understand the origin of volitional formations; they do not understand the cessation of volitional formations; they do not understand the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations.

They do not understand these phenomena; they do not understand the origin of these phenomena; they do not understand the cessation of these phenomena; they do not understand the way leading to the cessation of these phenomena.
Monks, those recluses or brahmins are not, among recluses, reckoned as recluses, nor among brahmins, reckoned as brahmins.

They are esteemed as brahmins, yet those venerable ones do not, by realizing it for themselves with direct knowledge, enter and dwell in the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood in this very life.
But, bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins understand these things, of those things—
They understand their arising; they understand the cessation of these phenomena;
they understand the way leading to the cessation of these phenomena. What phenomena do they understand? Of what phenomena do they understand the arising?
Of what phenomena do they understand the cessation? Of what phenomena do they understand the way leading to cessation?

They understand aging-and-death, they understand the origin of aging-and-death, they understand the cessation of aging-and-death, and they understand the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death; [they understand] birth...
existence... [and so on].
clinging … craving … feeling …
Contact … the six sense bases … name-and-form …
They understand consciousness...

they understand volitional formations, they understand the origin of volitional formations, they understand the cessation of volitional formations, and they understand the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations.

They understand these phenomena, they understand the origin of these phenomena, they understand the cessation of these phenomena, and they understand the way leading to the cessation of these phenomena.
“Those ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, are indeed recognized as ascetics among ascetics and as brahmins among brahmins;
and those venerable ones, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life the goal of the ascetic life and the goal of the brahmin life, enter and dwell therein.”
