The Discourse to Kaccānagotta.
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Kaccānagotta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘right view, right view.
In what way, venerable sir, is there right view?
“Kaccāna, this world generally relies on a duality: ‘it exists’ and ‘it does not exist.’”
“Kaccāna, for one who sees the arising of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no ‘non-existence’ regarding the world.
Kaccāna, for one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no ‘existence’ regarding the world.
For this world, Kaccāna, is for the most part bound by attachment, clinging, and adherence.”

And he does not approach, does not cling to, does not resolve upon, and does not underlie with a latent tendency toward this pursuit, this clinging, this mental fixation, and this adherence, thinking:
"This is my self. He neither doubts nor wavers, thinking: "Only suffering arises when it arises; only suffering ceases when it ceases. In this matter, his knowledge is independent of others.
It is to this extent, Kaccāna, that there is right view.
‘Everything exists,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme.
‘Nothing exists’ is the second extreme.
Without approaching either of these two extremes, Kaccāna, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way:
‘With ignorance as condition,
volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition,
consciousness arises …pe… such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.’
"But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."
Fifth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.16 (SN 12.16, PTS SN ii 18) 2.
Āhāravagga (The Chapter on Nutriments)
The Discourse on the Preacher of the Dhamma.
At Sāvatthī...
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘a Dhamma-speaker, a Dhamma-speaker.
To what extent, venerable sir, is one a Dhamma-speaker?
“If, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with aging-and-death, for its fading away and cessation, he may be called a ‘bhikkhu who is a Dhamma-speaker.’”

If a bhikkhu is practicing for the sake of disenchantment with aging-and-death, for its fading away, and for its cessation, it is sufficient to say of him: “This bhikkhu is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.

If a bhikkhu, through disenchantment with aging-and-death, through its fading away, and through its cessation, is liberated by non-clinging, it is sufficient to say of him: “This bhikkhu has attained Nibbāna in this very life. [The same applies] if a bhikkhu [is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, fading away, and cessation] with respect to birth... [and so on].
If a bhikkhu [is weary] of existence...
if a bhikkhu [is weary] of clinging...
if a bhikkhu [is weary] of craving...
If a bhikkhu [is not repelled] by feeling … if a bhikkhu [is not repelled] by contact … if a bhikkhu [is not repelled] by the six sense bases …
If, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu [is disenchanted with] name-and-form...
if, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu [is disenchanted with] consciousness...
if, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu [is disenchanted with] volitional formations...
“If a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with ignorance, for its fading away, and for its cessation, he is fit to be called a ‘bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma.
If a bhikkhu practices for the sake of disenchantment with ignorance, for its fading away, and for its cessation, he is fit to be called a ‘bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.

If a bhikkhu, through disenchantment with ignorance, through its fading away, and through its cessation, is liberated by non-clinging, he is fit to be called a ‘bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’”
Sixth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.17 (SN 12.17, PTS SN ii 18) 2.
Āhāravagga (The Chapter on Nutriments)
The Discourse to Acelaka Kassapa.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One:
“We would ask the venerable Gotama about a certain matter, if the venerable Gotama would grant us the opportunity for an answer to our question.
“It is not yet the right time for a question, Kassapa,” [the Blessed One replied].
“We have entered among the houses.
A second time, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One:
“We would ask the venerable Gotama about a certain point, if the venerable Gotama would grant us the opportunity for an answer to our question.”
“Kassapa, this is not yet the time for a question;
we have entered among the houses.
A third time, the naked ascetic Kassapa... [as before]...
“We have entered among the houses.
When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One:
“It is not that we wish to question Master Gotama on many points.”
“Ask, Kassapa, whatever you wish,” [the Blessed One said].
“Is it the case, Master Gotama, that suffering is self-made?
“Not so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One replied.
“But, Master Gotama, is suffering created by another?
“Not so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One said.
“Then, Master Gotama, is suffering created both by oneself and by another?”
“Do not say so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One said.
“But, Master Gotama, does suffering arise without being made by oneself, without being made by another, and through spontaneous occurrence?
“Do not say so, Kassapa,” the Blessed One said.
“Master Gotama, is it that there is no suffering?
“Kassapa, it is not that there is no suffering.
There is indeed suffering, Kassapa.”
"In that case, Master Gotama does not know suffering and does not see it.
"Kassapa, it is not that I do not know suffering or do not see it.
Kassapa, I do indeed know suffering; I do indeed see suffering."
“I do indeed see suffering, Kassapa.
“But, Master Gotama, when asked, ‘Is suffering created by oneself? you say, ‘Do not say so, Kassapa.
And when asked, ‘Then is suffering created by another? you say, ‘Do not say so, Kassapa.’”
“When you were asked, ‘Master Gotama, is suffering both self-made and made by another? you said, ‘Do not say so, Kassapa.
When you were asked, ‘But Master Gotama, is suffering neither self-made nor made by another, but arisen fortuitously?
you said, ‘Do not say so, Kassapa. When you were asked, ‘Master Gotama, does suffering not exist? you said, ‘Kassapa, it is not that suffering does not exist; indeed, Kassapa, suffering exists.’”
“Then, when asked, ‘Does Master Gotama not know and not see suffering? you replied, ‘Indeed, Kassapa, it is not that I do not know or do not see suffering.
I do know suffering, Kassapa; I do see suffering, Kassapa.’”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One explain suffering to me;
let the Blessed One teach me about suffering.
“Kassapa, for one who asserts from the outset that ‘the one who acts is the one who experiences,’ saying ‘suffering is self-made,’ this leads to eternalism.”
“‘One person acts and another experiences [the result],’ Kassapa—when one is thus pierced by feeling, to say ‘suffering is caused by another’ is to fall into the view of annihilationism.
Without approaching either of these two extremes, Kassapa, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by way of the middle:
‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;”
With volitional formations as condition,
consciousness arises …pe… such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;
“With the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on] ...thus is there a cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways.
I go for refuge, Bhante, to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
“Venerable sir, may I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive the full ordination.
“Kassapa, whoever was formerly a member of another sect who desires the going-forth and desires the full ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline must undergo a four-month probationary period.
At the end of those four months, if the monks are satisfied with his mind...”
“They give him the going-forth and ordain him for the state of a bhikkhu.
Moreover, Bhante, I know the distinction between individuals.
“If, Bhante, one who was formerly a member of another sect desires the going-forth in this Dhamma and Vinaya, desires [ordination]…”
“For full ordination, one undergoes a probationary period of four months.
At the end of those four months, if the bhikkhus are pleased, they grant the going forth and confer full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu. I shall undergo a probationary period of four years;
at the end of those four years, if the bhikkhus are pleased, let them grant me the going forth and confer full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu.”
The naked ascetic Kassapa received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.

Not long after his ordination, the Venerable Kassapa, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time attained that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—the unsurpassed consummation of the spiritual life.
Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein.
He understood: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And thus the Venerable Kassapa became one of the Arahants.
Seventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.18 (SN 12.18, PTS SN ii 22) 2.
Āhāravagga (The Chapter on Nutriments)
The Timbaruka Sutta.
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.
Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Timbaruka said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain created by oneself?
"Do not say that, Timbaruka," the Blessed One replied.
"But, Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain created by another?
"Not so, Timbaruka," the Blessed One said.
"Then, Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain both self-created and created by another?"
"Do not say so, Timbaruka," the Blessed One said.
"But, Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain not self-made, not made by another, but arisen fortuitously?
"Do not say so, Timbaruka," the Blessed One said.
"Master Gotama, is it that there is neither pleasure nor pain?
"There is not, Timbaruka, neither pleasure nor pain;
rather, Timbaruka, there is both pleasure and pain."
"In that case, Master Gotama, does he not know and not see pleasure and pain?
"Indeed, Timbaruka, it is not that I do not know or do not see pleasure and pain.
I do, Timbaruka, know pleasure and pain."
“I do indeed see pleasure and pain, Timbaruka.
“Master Gotama, when asked, ‘Is pleasure and pain created by oneself? you replied, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.
But when asked, ‘Then is pleasure and pain created by another? you replied, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.’”
“When you were asked, ‘Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain both self-made and made by another? you said, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.
When you were asked, ‘But Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain neither self-made nor made by another, but arisen fortuitously? you said, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.
When you were asked, ‘Then, Master Gotama, is there no pleasure and pain? you said, ‘Timbaruka, it is not that there is no pleasure and pain.’”
“Timbaruka, you say, ‘There indeed is pleasure and pain.
When asked, ‘In that case, Master Gotama neither knows nor sees pleasure and pain,’ you replied: ‘No, Timbaruka, it is not that I do not know or see pleasure and pain.
I do indeed, Timbaruka, know pleasure and pain;’”
“I see pleasure and pain, Timbaruka,” you say.
“May the venerable Gotama explain pleasure and pain to me;
may the venerable Gotama teach me about pleasure and pain.”
“‘That is the feeling, that is the feeler,’ Timbaruka—regarding what exists from the beginning, I do not say in this way that ‘pleasure and pain are self-made.
‘The feeling is one thing, the feeler is another,’ Timbaruka—regarding one who is pierced by feeling, I do not say in this way that ‘pleasure and pain are made by another.
Without approaching either of these two extremes, Timbaruka, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way:”
‘With ignorance as condition,
volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition,
consciousness arises …pe… such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.’
"But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."
When this was said, the wanderer Timbaruka said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
This was the eighth [sutta]. Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.19 (SN 12.19, PTS SN ii 23).
2. Āhāravagga:
Bālapaṇḍitasutta.
At Sāvatthī he was staying.
“Bhikkhus, for the fool hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has come to be in such a way.

Thus, this body and external name-and-form—this is the dyad. Dependent upon this dyad, there is contact, namely the six sense bases, through which the fool experiences pleasure and pain, or one or another of them.
Bhikkhus, for the wise person hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has come to be in such a way.”

"Thus, this body and external name-and-form—this is the dyad. Dependent upon this dyad, there is contact, which consists of the six sense bases; touched by these, or by one or another of them, the wise person experiences pleasure and pain.
In this regard, monks, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what is the disparity between the wise person and the fool?
"Bhante, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be well..."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One himself explain the meaning of this statement; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, that ignorance by which the fool is shrouded and that craving with which he is associated—by means of these, this body has come to be. That very ignorance of the fool has not been abandoned, and that craving has not been exhausted.
For what reason? [Because]...”
“Monks, the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering.
Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool goes to a state of being;
having gone to a state of being, he is not liberated from birth, aging, and death, nor from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”
"I say that he is not liberated from suffering.

For, monks, that ignorance by which the wise man was shrouded and that craving with which he was associated—through which this body came to be—both that ignorance has been abandoned by the wise man and that craving has been utterly exhausted.
And for what reason?"
"Monks, the wise person practices the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering.
Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the wise person does not become subject to a body.
Not becoming subject to a body, he is liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs."
"I say that one is liberated from suffering.
This, monks, is the distinction, this is the underlying purpose, this is the difference between a wise person and a fool, namely, the living of the holy life.
Thus ends the ninth discourse.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.20 (SN 12.20, PTS SN ii 25) 2. Āhāravagga Paccayasutta (The Discourse on Conditions) “Monks, I shall teach you conditions and the conditioned. Listen to that and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, monks, is a condition, and what is the conditioned? Dependent on ignorance, volitional formations [come to be]; dependent on volitional formations, consciousness; dependent on consciousness, name-and-form; dependent on name-and-form, the six sense bases; dependent on the six sense bases, contact; dependent on contact, feeling; dependent on feeling, craving; dependent on craving, clinging; dependent on clinging, existence; dependent on existence, birth; dependent on birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is called a condition, and this is called the conditioned. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is called a condition, and this is called the conditioned.”
Staying at Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One said]:
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and dependently arisen phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppanna-dhammā*).
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?”
“With birth as condition, monks, there is aging-and-death.
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this element remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena, specific conditionality.
A Tathāgata awakens to this and penetrates it.”
Having fully awakened to it and realized it, he declares, teaches, makes known, establishes, reveals, analyzes, and clarifies it.
And he says: "Behold, monks, conditioned by birth, there is aging and death."
“With existence as condition, monks, there is birth...
With clinging as condition, monks, there is existence...
With craving as condition, monks, there is clinging.”
“With feeling as condition, monks, craving arises… with contact as condition, monks,
feeling arises… with the six sense bases as condition, monks, contact arises.”
“Monks, with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
monks, with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises;
monks, with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises.”

“Bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise—whether Tathāgatas appear or do not appear. That element remains fixed: the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena, specific conditionality.
The Tathāgata awakens to this and penetrates it.”
Having fully awakened to it and realized it, he declares, teaches, proclaims, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and clarifies it.
And he says: "Behold, monks!
Conditioned by ignorance, monks, are volitional formations."
Thus, monks, that which therein is suchness, non-falsity, non-otherness, and specific conditionality— this, monks,
is called dependent origination. And what, monks,
are the dependently originated phenomena?
“Monks, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Birth, monks, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Becoming, monks, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.”
Clinging, monks, ...
craving, monks, ...
feeling, monks, ... [is conditioned by contact].
Contact, monks… the six sense bases,
monks… name-and-form, monks…
Consciousness, bhikkhus… volitional formations, bhikkhus… ignorance, bhikkhus, are impermanent,
conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
“Monks, these are called dependently arisen phenomena.

When, monks, for a noble disciple this dependent origination and these dependently arisen phenomena have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom, he will certainly not run back toward the past, thinking:
‘Did I exist in the past? Or did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past?’”
‘How indeed was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past?
Or he will pursue the future:
‘Shall I indeed exist in the future? Or shall I not exist in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future?
Having been what, what shall I become in the future?’
Or in the present time, it is impossible that one would be internally full of doubt, thinking:
"Do I exist? Or do I not exist? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? And where will it go?"—this situation does not occur.
"And for what reason?
Because, monks, this dependent origination and these dependently arisen phenomena have been well seen by the noble disciple with right wisdom, exactly as they are.
The tenth.
The second chapter: On Nutriment.
Its summary verse:
Nutriment and Phagguna, indeed.
And two ascetics and brahmins:
Kaccānagotta the preacher of the Dhamma,
and Acela Timbaruka.
The fool and the wise man,
and tenthly, by way of condition.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12.21 (SN 12.21, PTS SN ii 27).
3. The Chapter on the Ten Powers.
Discourse on the Ten Powers.
[The Blessed One] was dwelling at Sāvatthī.

“Endowed, monks, with the ten powers and endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence, the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel:
‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling, such its origin, such its passing away.’”
Such is perception, such is the arising of perception, such is the passing away of perception;
such are volitional formations, such is the arising of volitional formations, such is the passing away of volitional formations;
such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.
Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises ...
[and so on] ... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; ... [and so on] ... such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
“With the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
The first.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.22 (SN 12.22, PTS SN ii 28) 3. Dasabalavagga Dutiyadasabalasutta (The Second Discourse on the Ten Powers) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessing which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader of the herd, utters his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the brahma wheel. What ten? (1) Here, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. This is the first power of a Tathāgata... (2) He understands as it really is the result of the undertaking of kamma past, future, and present in terms of possibilities and causes. This is the second power of a Tathāgata... (3) He understands as it really is the various elements in the world with their many and different elements. This is the third power of a Tathāgata... (4) He understands as it really is the diversity in the dispositions of beings. This is the fourth power of a Tathāgata... (5) He understands as it really is the way leading anywhere to the attainment of all modes of perception. This is the fifth power of a Tathāgata... (6) He understands as it really is the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence in regard to the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. This is the sixth power of a Tathāgata... (7) He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of world-dissolution and evolution: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. This is the seventh power of a Tathāgata... (8) With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right views, and undertook actions based on right views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, even in the heavenly world. Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This is the eighth power of a Tathāgata... (9) By realizing for himself with direct knowledge, the Tathāgata here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. This is the ninth power of a Tathāgata... (10) The Tathāgata understands as it really is the destruction and non-arising of all phenomena through the destruction of craving. This is the tenth power of a Tathāgata... Possessing these ten powers of a Tathāgata, the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader of the herd, utters his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the brahma wheel.”
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.

"Monks, endowed with the ten powers and endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence, the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel:
'Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.'"
Such is feeling, such is the arising of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling;
such is perception, such is the arising of perception, such is the passing away of perception;
such are volitional formations, such is the arising of volitional formations, such is the passing away of volitional formations.
"Such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.
Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases."
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises...
and so on... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations;
with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness ...
[and so on] ... in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’
“Thus, monks, has the Dhamma been well-expounded by me—clear, open, revealed, with its shrouds cut away.
Since the Dhamma has been thus well-expounded by me, clear, open, revealed, with its shrouds cut away, it is enough for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith to arouse energy, thinking:

‘Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood dry up in my body. But as long as I have not attained what can be reached through human firmness, vigor, and effort, I shall not abandon my effort.’”
‘That which is to be attained by human strength, human energy, and human exertion— until that is reached, there will be no stopping of one’s effort.
Monks, it is painful to dwell lazy, mired in evil and unwholesome states, and one thus fails to achieve the great goal of one’s own welfare.
But one who has aroused energy, monks, dwells happily, secluded from evil, unwholesome states, and fulfills his own great goal.
Monks, the attainment of the supreme is not achieved by the inferior;
rather, monks, the attainment of the supreme is achieved by the supreme.
“Bhikkhus, this holy life is one that can be drunk up, with the Teacher standing right before you.
Therefore, bhikkhus, arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the direct experience of the as-yet-unexperienced:
‘In this way, our going forth shall not be barren; it shall be fruitful and fertile.’”
‘And for those from whom we enjoy robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, their acts of service toward us will become of great fruit and great benefit’—
in this way, monks, you should train yourselves. For, monks,
when one considers one’s own welfare, it is indeed sufficient to strive with diligence to achieve it.
“Indeed, bhikkhus, for one who perceives the welfare of others, it is sufficient to strive with diligence;
indeed, bhikkhus, for one who perceives the welfare of both, it is sufficient to strive with diligence. This is the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.23 (SN 12.23, PTS SN ii 29) 3. Dasabalavagga Upanisāsutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four conditions for the arising of the unarisen Noble Eightfold Path, and for the growth and fulfillment by development of the Noble Eightfold Path once it has arisen. What four? Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the four conditions for the arising of the unarisen Noble Eightfold Path, and for the growth and fulfillment by development of the Noble Eightfold Path once it has arisen.”
Staying at Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One said]:
“Monks, I declare that the destruction of the taints occurs for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see.
And what, monks, is it that one must know and see for the destruction of the taints to occur?”
"Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling ... [and so on] ... such is perception ..."
"Thus are volitional formations...
thus is consciousness, thus is the arising of consciousness, thus is the passing away of consciousness.
It is for one who knows thus and sees thus, monks, that the destruction of the taints occurs.
“Bhikkhus, that knowledge of destruction regarding destruction, I say, has a proximate cause; it is not without a proximate cause.
And what, bhikkhus, is the proximate cause for the knowledge of destruction?
‘Liberation,’ it should be said.”
“Monks, I say that liberation has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause for liberation?
It should be said: ‘Dispassion.’”
“Monks, I say that dispassion has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of dispassion?
It should be said: ‘Disenchantment.’”
“Monks, I say that disenchantment has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of disenchantment?
It should be said: ‘Knowledge and vision according to reality.’”
“Monks, I say that knowledge and vision of things as they truly are has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause for knowledge and vision of things as they truly are?
It should be said: ‘Concentration.’”
“Monks, I say that concentration has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of concentration?
It should be said: ‘Happiness.’”
“Bhikkhus, I say that pleasure has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, bhikkhus, is the proximate cause of pleasure?
‘Tranquillity,’ it should be said.”
“Monks, I say that tranquility has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of tranquility?
It should be said: ‘Rapture.’”
“Monks, I say that rapture has a proximate cause; it is not without a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of rapture?
It should be said: ‘Joy.’”
“Monks, I say that gladness has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of gladness?
It should be said: ‘Faith.’”
“Monks, I say that faith has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of faith?
It should be said: ‘Suffering.’”
"Bhikkhus, I say that suffering too has a proximate cause; it is not without a proximate cause.
And what, bhikkhus, is the proximate cause of suffering?
It should be said: 'Birth.'"
“Monks, I say that birth has a proximate cause; it is not without a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of birth?
It should be said: ‘Existence.’”
“Bhikkhus, I say that existence has a proximate cause; it does not exist without a proximate cause.
And what, bhikkhus, is the proximate cause of existence?
It should be said: ‘Clinging.’”
“Monks, I say that clinging also has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of clinging?
It should be said: ‘Craving.’”
“Monks, craving also, I say, has a proximate cause; it does not lack a proximate cause.
And what, monks, is the proximate cause of craving?
It should be said: ‘Feeling. …”
‘Contact,’ it should be said … ‘The six sense bases,’ it should be said … ‘Name-and-form,’ it should be said …
‘Consciousness,’ it should be said...
‘Volitional formations,’ it should be said.
“I say, bhikkhus, that volitional formations have a proximate cause, not that they are without a proximate cause.”
"And what, monks, is the proximate cause for volitional formations?
'Ignorance,' it should be said.
Thus, monks, ignorance is the proximate cause for volitional formations."
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases.
With the six sense bases as its proximate cause is contact;
with contact as its proximate cause is feeling;
with feeling as its proximate cause is craving.
With craving as its proximate cause is clinging;
with clinging as its proximate cause is existence;
with existence as its proximate cause is birth.
Suffering has birth as its proximate cause;
faith has suffering as its proximate cause;
joy has faith as its proximate cause.
Rapture has gladness as its proximate cause;
tranquility has rapture as its proximate cause;
happiness has tranquility as its proximate cause.
Concentration has happiness as its proximate cause;
knowledge and vision of things as they really are has concentration as its proximate cause;
disenchantment has knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its proximate cause.
Dispassion has disenchantment as its proximate cause;
liberation has dispassion as its proximate cause;
and the knowledge of destruction has liberation as its proximate cause.
“Just as, monks, when it rains in thick drops from a cloud high above the mountains, that water, flowing down according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, gullies, and creeks;
when the mountain clefts, gullies, and creeks are full, they fill the small pools;
when the small pools are full, they fill the large pools; when the large pools are full—”
The rivulets fill up; the filled rivulets fill up the great rivers; the filled great rivers fill up the great ocean.
Even so, monks, with ignorance as a condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as a condition, consciousness; with consciousness as a condition...

Name-and-form; with name-and-form as its condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as their condition, contact; with contact as its condition, feeling; with feeling as its condition, craving;
with craving as its condition, clinging; with clinging as its condition, existence; with existence as its condition, birth; with birth as its condition, suffering;
with suffering as its condition, faith; with faith as its condition, gladness; with gladness as its condition, rapture;
“Tranquility has serenity as its proximate cause; happiness has tranquility as its proximate cause; concentration has happiness as its proximate cause;
knowledge and vision of things as they really are has concentration as its proximate cause; disenchantment has knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its proximate cause;
dispassion has disenchantment as its proximate cause; liberation has dispassion as its proximate cause; and the knowledge of destruction has liberation as its proximate cause.”
Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.24 (SN 12.24, PTS SN ii 32) 3.
Dasabalavagga (The Chapter on the Ten Powers)
The Discourse on Other Sectarians.
While staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove,
the Venerable Sāriputta dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha.
What if I were to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects reside?"
Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the park of certain wanderers of other sects. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said this to him:
"Friend Sāriputta, there are certain recluses and brahmins who are proponents of action and who describe suffering as being self-made."
"Furthermore, friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering is caused by another.
There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering is caused both by oneself and by another.

Furthermore, friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering arises fortuitously, being caused neither by oneself nor by another."
"But here, friend Sāriputta, what does the ascetic Gotama say,
and what does he proclaim? And how, in answering, would we be speaking exactly as the ascetic Gotama speaks,
not misrepresenting the ascetic Gotama with what is untrue, and answering in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no one..."
“Would one fall into a position that is consistent with the Dhamma and subject to censure?
“Suffering, friend, has been described by the Blessed One as dependently arisen.
Dependent upon what?”
"Dependent upon contact.

Speaking thus, one would be a speaker of what was said by the Blessed One, and one would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue; one would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable objection could be found to warrant blame.
In this regard, friends, as for those recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action and proclaim that suffering is self-made—that too is conditioned by contact.
Whatever recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action proclaim that suffering is caused by another, that too is conditioned by contact.
Whatever recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action proclaim that suffering is both self-caused and caused by another, that too is conditioned by contact.
Whatever recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action proclaim that suffering arises fortuitously, being neither self-caused nor caused by another, that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, friends, as for those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action and proclaim that suffering is self-made—it is impossible that they will experience it apart from contact.
And as for those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action and proclaim that suffering is made by another—it is impossible that they will experience it apart from contact.

“Furthermore, those recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of karma and proclaim that suffering is both self-made and made by another—it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact.

And those recluses and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of karma and proclaim that suffering arises fortuitously, being neither self-made nor made by another—it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact.”
The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the Venerable Sāriputta and those wanderers of other sects.

Then, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from his almsround after the meal, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Sāriputta and those wanderers of other sects.
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! It is just as Sāriputta would speak when speaking correctly.
For I have said, Ānanda, that suffering is dependently arisen.”
"Based on what?
"Based on contact.

Speaking thus, one would be a speaker of what has been said by me; one would not misrepresent me with what is untrue; one would explain in accordance with the Dhamma; and no legitimate objection could be raised against one's position such that it would be subject to censure.

In this regard, Ānanda, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action and proclaim that suffering is self-made—this too is conditioned by contact. Those [who proclaim it is other-made]... [and so on]... those [who proclaim it is both self-made and other-made]... [and so on]... [all these are conditioned by contact].

“Furthermore, Ānanda, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of kamma and proclaim that suffering arises by chance—neither self-made nor made by another—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, Ānanda, as for those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of kamma and proclaim that suffering is self-made, it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact. As for those... [and so on]”

And as for those recluses and brahmins who proclaim that suffering arises by chance—neither self-made nor made by another—they cannot possibly experience it apart from contact; such a thing is impossible.
Once, Ānanda, I was staying right here in Rājagaha, at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Rājagaha for alms.
It occurred to me, Ānanda:
"It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha."
"What if I were to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects reside?
Then, Ānanda, I went to the park where the wanderers of other sects resided. Having arrived, I exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
When we had concluded our polite and courteous conversation, I sat down to one side. As I was sitting there, Ānanda, those wanderers of other sects said this to me:
“Venerable Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering is self-made.
There are, however, Venerable Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering is made by another.
There are, Venerable Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering is both self-made and made by another.”
"But there are, friend Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of karma and who declare that suffering arises fortuitously, being neither made by oneself nor made by another.
In this matter, what is the Venerable Gotama’s doctrine?
What does he proclaim? And how answering would we be speaking in accordance with the Venerable Gotama, and not contradicting him?"
‘...we would misrepresent Gotama with what is untrue, we would explain in accordance with the Dhamma,
and no legitimate point of criticism could be found to bring us into reproach’?
When this was said, Ānanda, I said this to those wanderers of other sects:
“Suffering, friend, has been described by me as dependently arisen.
Dependent upon what?
Dependent upon contact.”

"By speaking thus, one would be saying what has been said by me, and would not misrepresent me with what is false; one would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable objection could be found to warrant a censure.

In this regard, friends, as for those recluses and brahmins who advocate the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering is self-made—that too is conditioned by contact. And as for those... [and so on].
Those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim the doctrine of action, yet maintain that suffering arises by chance—neither self-made nor made by another—that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, friends, as for those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim the doctrine of action and maintain that suffering is self-made: it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact.
“Whether they be those ... [as before] ...

or those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim that suffering arises fortuitously, neither self-made nor made by another—that it has arisen by chance—it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact.”
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
For how could the entire meaning be expressed by a single word?
Might this same meaning, when spoken in detail, be both profound and appear profound?”
“Therefore, Ānanda, let what occurs to you on this matter be spoken.
“If, Bhante, they were to ask me:
‘Friend Ānanda, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the arising of aging-and-death?’”
“Venerable sir, if I were asked this, I would answer thus:
‘Old age and death, friend, have birth as their source, birth as their origin; they are born from birth and originate from birth.
Venerable sir, if I were asked this, I would answer thus.”
“Venerable sir, if they were to ask me thus:
‘But friend Ānanda, what is the source of birth, what is its origin, from what is it born, and from what does it arise?’—
being asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer thus:”
“‘Birth, friend, has its source in existence, its origin in existence, it is born from existence, it arises from existence.
Thus, Bhante, being asked, I would answer.
If, Bhante, they were to ask me this:”
"But, friend Ānanda, what is the source of existence, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its arising?
"If I were asked this, Bhante, I would answer thus:
'Existence, friend, has clinging as its source, clinging as its origin, clinging as its birth, clinging as its arising.'"
“Venerable sir, if I were asked thus, I would answer thus.
Venerable sir, if they were to ask me:
‘But, friend, what is clinging? …”
"But craving, friends...
feeling, friends... if, venerable sir, they were to ask me thus: [what is the origin of this suffering]?"
“But, friend Ānanda, what is the source of contact, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its arising?
“If I am asked this, Bhante, I would answer thus:
‘Contact, friend, has the six sense bases as its source, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its birth, the six sense bases as its arising.’”
"Friend, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of the six bases for contact, there is the cessation of contact;
with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving."
With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence;
with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth.
"With the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Venerable sir, if I were asked thus, I would answer in such a way.
The Fourth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.25 (SN 12.25, PTS SN ii 37) 3.
Dasabalavagga
The Bhūmija Sutta. At Sāvatthī.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Bhūmija emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Bhūmija said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that pleasure and pain are created by oneself.
But, friend Sāriputta, there are also some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that pleasure and pain are created by another."
"Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by another.

But there are also, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who profess the doctrine of action and maintain that pleasure and pain arise fortuitously, being neither self-made nor made by another.
Now, friend Sāriputta, what does the Blessed One here say, and how does he declare it?"
"And how, by answering thus, would we be speakers of what was said by the Blessed One,
not misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is false, answering in accordance with the Dhamma,
so that no one following the Dhamma could find ground for censure?"
“Friend, the Blessed One has said that pleasure and pain are dependently arisen.
Dependent upon what?
Dependent upon contact.”

Speaking thus, one would be a speaker of what was said by the Blessed One, and one would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false; one would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable objection could be found to warrant blame.

In this regard, friends, as for those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action and proclaim that pleasure and pain are self-made—that too has contact as its condition. And as for those... [and so on].
“Furthermore, friends,

those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim the doctrine of karma and maintain that pleasure and pain arise by chance— neither self-made nor made by another— that too is conditioned by contact. In this regard, friends,
as for those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim the doctrine of karma and maintain that pleasure and pain are self-made, it is impossible that they could experience them apart from contact.”
"Whether they be those ... [as before] ...
or those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim that pleasure and pain arise by chance, neither self-made nor made by another—it is impossible that they could experience them apart from contact."
The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Bhūmija.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entirety of the conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Bhūmija.
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! It is just as Sāriputta would speak when speaking rightly.
For I have said, Ānanda, that pleasure and pain are dependently arisen.
In dependence on what?”
"Dependent upon contact.

One who speaks thus would be a speaker of what has been said by me; he would not misrepresent me with what is false, he would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate point of criticism could be found to bring reproach upon him.
In this regard, Ānanda, those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action and proclaim that pleasure and pain are self-made—those too are conditioned by contact.
Whatever recluses and brahmins there may be who proclaim that pleasure and pain arise by chance— neither caused by oneself nor caused by another— that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, Ānanda, as for those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of karma and proclaim that pleasure and pain are self-made—it is impossible that they could experience them apart from contact. And as for those [who proclaim they are other-made]... and as for those [who proclaim they are both self-made and other-made]... it is impossible that they could experience them apart from contact.

As for those ascetics and brahmins who maintain the doctrine of action and proclaim that pleasure and pain arise fortuitously—neither made by oneself nor made by another—it is impossible that they will experience them apart from contact.
For when there is a body, Ānanda, it is with volition regarding the body as cause that pleasure and pain arise within;
or when there is speech, Ānanda, it is with volition regarding speech as cause that pleasure and pain arise within.
"Or else, Ānanda, with the mind as a condition, mental volition arises, and on account of that, pleasure and pain arise within oneself, conditioned by ignorance.
Or else, Ānanda, one personally performs that bodily formation because of which pleasure and pain arise within oneself.
Or else, Ānanda, others perform that bodily formation because of which pleasure and pain arise within oneself."
Either with full awareness, Ānanda, one performs that bodily formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for one;
or without full awareness, Ānanda, one performs that bodily formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for one.
Or, Ānanda, one personally performs that verbal formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for one.
Or others, Ānanda, perform that verbal formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for him.
Whether he is fully aware, Ānanda,
or whether he is not fully aware, Ānanda, he performs that verbal formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for him.
Either, Ānanda, one himself performs that mental volitional formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for him;
or others, Ānanda, perform that mental volitional formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for him;
or, Ānanda, one does so with full awareness... [and so on].
Or, Ānanda, one who is lacking clear comprehension performs that mental volitional formation conditioned by which internal pleasure and pain arise for him.
Ignorance, Ānanda, underlies these phenomena.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, Ānanda, that body does not exist, nor does that [feeling] arise conditioned by it.
“Internal pleasure and pain: there is no such speech as a condition for the arising of that internal pleasure and pain;
there is no such mind as a condition for the arising of that internal pleasure and pain.
There is no such field … no such site … no such sense-base … no such basis as a condition for the arising of that internal pleasure and pain.”
The Fifth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.26 (SN 12.26, PTS SN ii 41) 3.
Dasabalavagga (The Chapter on the Ten Powers)
The Upavāṇa Sutta.
The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upavāṇa said this to the Blessed One:
“But, venerable sir, there are some recluses and brahmins who proclaim suffering to be self-made;
there are some recluses and brahmins, venerable sir, who proclaim suffering to be made by another;
and there are some recluses and brahmins, venerable sir, who proclaim suffering to be both self-made and made by another.”
“But there are, venerable sir, some recluses and brahmins who proclaim suffering to be produced by chance— neither caused by oneself nor caused by another. In this matter, venerable sir,
what does the Blessed One say, what does he declare, and how would we have to answer so that we might be speaking in accordance with the Blessed One’s words,
not misrepresenting him with what is false, and in conformity with the Dhamma?”
“...could we explain it in such a way that no legitimate objection would lead to a ground for censure?
“Upavāṇa, suffering has been described by me as dependently arisen.
In dependence on what?”
“Dependent upon contact.

One who speaks thus would be saying what has been said by me, and would not misrepresent me with what is false; he would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable objection could be found to place him in a position of blame.
In this regard, Upavāṇa, those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim that suffering is self-made—that too is conditioned by contact.
Whatever ascetics and brahmins there may be who proclaim suffering to be produced by chance— neither caused by oneself nor caused by another— that too is conditioned by contact.

In this regard, Upavāṇa, as for those recluses and brahmins who proclaim that suffering is self-made, it is impossible that they will experience it apart from contact. And as for those... [and] as for those...
[and] as for those... [the same applies].
“Even those ascetics and brahmins who proclaim that suffering arises fortuitously, neither made by oneself nor made by another, it is impossible that they could experience it apart from contact.
The sixth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.27 (SN 12.27, PTS SN ii 42).
3. The Chapter on the Ten Powers:
The Discourse on Conditions. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“With ignorance as condition, monks, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition,
consciousness arises …pe… such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

And what, monks, is aging-and-death? The aging of those various beings in their respective classes of beings—their decrepitude, infirmity, broken teeth, graying hair, wrinkled skin, the decline of the life-span, and the decay of the faculties—this is called aging. And what is death? The passing away, the perishing, the breaking up, the disappearance, the dying, the completion of time, the dissolution of the aggregates, and the laying down of the body of those various beings in their respective classes of beings—this is called death.
This, monks, is called aging-and-death.

The passing away, the falling away, the breaking up, the disappearance, the death, the dying, the completion of time, the dissolution of the aggregates, the laying down of the body of this or that being from this or that class of beings—
this is called death. Thus, this aging and this death.
This, monks, is called aging-and-death.
With the arising of birth comes the arising of aging-and-death;
with the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging-and-death.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of aging and death.
That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
And what, monks, is birth? … [as before] …
And what, monks, is existence?
And what, monks, is clinging?
And what, monks, is craving?

At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
There the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Sāriputta, this was said in the *Pārāyana*, in the *Questions of Ajita*:
“Both those who have fully understood the Dhamma and the various trainees here—
of their conduct, may I, being wise, [know].”
“Being asked, please explain, dear sir.
“Sāriputta, how should the meaning of this brief statement be understood in detail?
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta remained silent.
A second time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta … [as before] … A second time,
the Venerable Sāriputta remained silent.
A third time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Sāriputta, this was said in the *Pārāyana*, in the *Ajitapañha*:
‘Those who have fully understood the Dhamma,
and those various trainees here;’”
“O Noble One, being asked, please tell me their prudent conduct.
“Sāriputta, how should the meaning of this brief statement be understood in detail?”
A third time, the Venerable Sāriputta remained silent.
“Do you see, Sāriputta, that ‘this has come to be’?
“Venerable sir, one sees with right wisdom, as it really is, that ‘this has come to be.’”
Having seen with right wisdom, as it really is, "This has come to be," one practices for disenchantment with what has come to be, for its fading away, and for its cessation.
One sees with right wisdom, as it really is, "Its origination is from nutriment.
Having seen with right wisdom, as it really is, "Its origination is from nutriment," one practices for disenchantment with its origination from nutriment, for its fading away, and for its cessation.
Then, through the cessation of that nutriment, one sees with correct wisdom, as it truly is, that "what has come to be is subject to cessation.

Having seen with correct wisdom, as it truly is, that "through the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation," one practices for disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of that which is subject to cessation.
In this way, venerable sir, one is a trainee.
And how, venerable sir, is one a person who has mastered the Dhamma?
One sees, venerable sir, with right wisdom according to reality: "This is what has come to be.

Having seen with right wisdom according to reality that "this is what has come to be," through disenchantment with what has come to be, through its fading away, through its cessation, one becomes liberated by non-clinging.
One sees with correct wisdom, as it truly is, that "this has its origin from nutriment.

Having seen with correct wisdom, as it truly is, that "this has its origin from nutriment," one becomes liberated through non-clinging by way of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding that which has its origin from nutriment.
One sees with correct wisdom, as it truly is, that "whatever has come to be because of the cessation of nutriment is subject to cessation."

Then, by the cessation of that nutriment, having seen with correct wisdom as it really is that "whatever has come to be is subject to cessation," one becomes liberated through non-clinging due to disenchantment with, fading away from, and the cessation of what is subject to cessation.
In this way, venerable sir, one is one who has comprehended the Dhamma.
Thus, venerable sir, regarding that which was said in the *Pārāyana*, in the questions of Ajita:
“Both those who have fully understood the Dhamma and the various trainees here—
of their conduct, may I, being wise, [know].”
“Being asked, please explain, dear sir.
“Venerable sir, this is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was stated by the Blessed One in brief:
‘One sees, as it really is, with correct wisdom, that "this has come to be. “Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! ‘This has come to be,’ Sāriputta—one sees this as it really is with correct wisdom.”
Having seen with right wisdom, as it truly is, "This has come to be," one practices for disenchantment with what has come to be, for its fading away, and for its cessation.
One sees with right wisdom, as it truly is, "Its origination is due to nutriment.

Having seen with right wisdom, as it truly is, "Its origination is due to nutriment," one practices for disenchantment with the origination due to nutriment, for its fading away, and for its cessation.
Then, through the cessation of that nutriment, one sees with correct wisdom, as it truly is, that "what has come to be is subject to cessation.

Having seen with correct wisdom, as it truly is, that "through the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation," one practices for disenchantment with, for the fading away of lust for, and for the cessation of that which is subject to cessation.
In this way, Sāriputta, one is a trainee.
And how, Sāriputta, is one one who has fathomed the Dhamma?
One sees with correct wisdom, as it really is: "This is what has come to be.

Having seen with correct wisdom, as it really is, that "this is what has come to be," one becomes liberated through non-clinging by means of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be.
One sees with correct wisdom, as it really is, that "this has its origin from nutriment.

Having seen with correct wisdom, as it really is, that "this has its origin from nutriment," one becomes liberated through non-clinging by means of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has its origin from nutriment.
One sees with correct wisdom, as it really is, that "whatever has come to be because of the cessation of nutriment is subject to cessation."

Then, by the cessation of that nutriment, seeing with right wisdom as it really is that "whatever has come to be is subject to cessation," one becomes liberated through non-clinging, due to disenchantment, dispassion, and the cessation of what is subject to cessation.
In this way, Sāriputta, one is one who has comprehended the Dhamma.
Thus, Sāriputta, regarding that which was said in the *Pārāyana*, in the *Ajitapañha*:
“Both those who have fully understood the Dhamma and the various trainees here—
of their conduct, may I, being wise, [learn].”
“Being asked, answer, dear sir.
This, Sāriputta, is how the meaning of what was said in brief by the Blessed One should be understood in detail. Thus ends the first [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.32 (SN 12.32, PTS SN ii 50) 4. Kaḷārakhattiyavagga Kaḷārasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Kaḷāra approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why among human beings some are short-lived and some long-lived; some have much sickness and some little sickness; some are ugly and some beautiful; some are low-born and some high-born; some are poor and some wealthy; some are lowly and some of noble birth? "Brahmin, beings are owners of their kamma, heirs of their kamma; they have kamma as their origin, kamma as their relative, kamma as their resort; whatever kamma they perform, whether good or bad, they become its heirs. "But, Master Gotama, how does a person become short-lived through their own kamma? How does a person become long-lived through their own kamma? How does a person become sickly... healthy... ugly... beautiful... low-born... high-born... poor... wealthy... lowly... of noble birth through their own kamma? "Brahmin, here a person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. Because of performing such deeds, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower world, or in hell. Having passed away from there, they are reborn among humans, and because of the remnants of that kamma, they become short-lived. This is how a person becomes short-lived through their own kamma. But here, brahmin, a person abstains from destroying life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. Because of performing such deeds, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Having passed away from there, they are reborn among humans, and because of the remnants of that kamma, they become long-lived. This is how a person becomes long-lived through their own kamma. [Similarly for the other traits. Furthermore, brahmin, here a person is one who, when asked, does not answer; when asked, they answer evasively; when asked, they answer falsely; when asked, they do not answer at all. Because of performing such deeds... they become low-born. This is how a person becomes low-born through their own kamma. But here, brahmin, a person is one who, when asked, answers; when asked, they do not answer evasively; when asked, they do not answer falsely; when asked, they answer fully. Because of performing such deeds... they become high-born. This is how a person becomes high-born through their own kamma. Furthermore, brahmin, here a person is stingy, miserly, and mean; they do not give food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, or lamps to those who ask. Because of performing such deeds... they become poor. This is how a person becomes poor through their own kamma. But here, brahmin, a person is not stingy, miserly, or mean; they give food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps to those who ask. Because of performing such deeds... they become wealthy. This is how a person becomes wealthy through their own kamma. Furthermore, brahmin, here a person is prone to anger and easily loses their temper; even when slightly criticized, they lose their temper, become resentful, and display ill will and hatred. Because of performing such deeds... they become lowly. This is how a person becomes lowly through their own kamma. But here, brahmin, a person is not prone to anger or easily losing their temper; even when severely criticized, they do not lose their temper, become resentful, or display ill will and hatred. Because of performing such deeds... they become of noble birth. This is how a person becomes of noble birth through their own kamma. When this was said, the brahmin Kaḷāra said to the Blessed One: "Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts."
Staying at Sāvatthī, the bhikkhu Kaḷārakhattiya approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the bhikkhu Kaḷārakhattiya said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, the bhikkhu Moḷiyaphagguna has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
“Surely that venerable one did not find comfort in this Dhamma and Discipline?
“Then, friend Sāriputta, have you found comfort in this Dhamma and Discipline?”
“I do not have doubt about this, friend,” he said.
“But will you have it in the future, friend?
“I do not have uncertainty about this, friend.”
Then the bhikkhu Kaḷārakhattiya rose from his seat, approached the Blessed One,
paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the bhikkhu Kaḷārakhattiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has declared final knowledge:
‘I understand: birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.

‘Friend Sāriputta, the Teacher calls you.

“If, Sāriputta, they were to ask you:

If you were asked this, Sāriputta, how would you answer?
“If they were to ask me this, Bhante:”
"But how, friend Sāriputta, knowing what and seeing what, was final knowledge declared by you:
'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being'?"—
if asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer thus:
‘Friends, when there is a cause for birth, with the destruction of that cause, it is known: “In what has been destroyed, I am destroyed.
Having known “I am destroyed,” one understands:
“Birth is exhausted; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been done; there is no more of this state of being.”’
“If asked thus, Bhante, I would answer in this way.
“But, Sāriputta, if they were to ask you:
‘Friend Sāriputta, what is the source of birth? What is its origin? From what is it born? What is its provenance?’”
“If you were asked this, Sāriputta, how would you answer?
“Venerable sir, if they were to ask me:
‘But friend Sāriputta, what is the source of birth, what is its origin, from what is it born, and from what does it arise?’”
“Being asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer:
‘Birth, friend, has existence as its source, existence as its origin; it is born of existence, it arises from existence.
Being asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer in this way.”
“But if, Sāriputta, they were to ask you:
‘But, friend Sāriputta, what is the source of existence (bhava)? What is its origin? Of what is it born?
From what does it arise?’—being asked thus, Sāriputta, how would you answer?”
“Venerable sir, if they were to ask me:
‘But friend Sāriputta, what is the source of existence, what is its origin, from what is it born, and from what does it arise?’—
being asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer thus:”
“‘Existence, friend, has its source in clinging, its origin in clinging, it is born of clinging, and it arises from clinging.
If asked thus, Bhante, I would answer in this way.
“But, Sāriputta, if they were to ask you this:”
"But as for clinging, friend...
[as before] ...But if, Sāriputta, they were to ask you:
'Friend Sāriputta, what is the source of craving, what is its origin, from what is it born, and from what does it arise? "
“If you were asked this, Sāriputta, how would you answer?
“Venerable sir, if they were to ask me:
‘But friend Sāriputta, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the arising of craving?’”
“Being asked thus, Bhante, I would answer:
‘Craving, friend, has feeling as its source, feeling as its origin, feeling as its birth, feeling as its arising.
Being asked thus, Bhante, I would answer in this way.”
“But if, Sāriputta, they were to ask you this:
‘Friend Sāriputta, how knowing and how seeing did that delight in feelings not arise in you?’—
being asked thus, Sāriputta, how would you answer?”
“Venerable sir, if they were to ask me:
‘Friend Sāriputta, how knowing and how seeing did that delight in feelings not arise in you?’—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer thus:
‘Friends, there are these three kinds of feeling.’”
Which three?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
These, friends, are the three feelings that are impermanent.
‘What is impermanent is suffering’—this is understood;
‘whatever delight there is in feelings, that has not arisen.
If asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer in this way.”
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
This too, Sāriputta, is a method for explaining this same point in brief:
‘Whatever is felt, that is included within suffering.’”
“But if, Sāriputta, they were to ask you this:
‘In what way, friend Sāriputta, was final knowledge declared by you:
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”?’”
“If you were asked this, Sāriputta, how would you answer?
“Venerable sir, if they were to ask me:
‘But in what way, friend Sāriputta, was final knowledge declared by you regarding the deliverances?’”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—this I understand.
If I were asked thus, venerable sir, I would answer thus:
‘Friends, through internal liberation and the destruction of all clinging, I dwell so mindful that the taints do not flow within me while I am dwelling mindfully, and I do not disparage myself.’”
“If asked thus, Bhante, I would answer in this way.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
This too, Sāriputta, is a method for explaining this same matter in brief.”
“I have no doubt regarding those taints spoken of by the ascetic; I do not waver that they have been abandoned by me.

and even if the Blessed One were to question me about this matter for seven days and nights using various terms and various methods,
I could explain this matter to the Blessed One for seven days and nights using various [terms and methods].
