But when, friends, the Blessed One approved my first question, it occurred to me:

"Even if the Blessed One were to ask me about this matter for an entire day using various words and various methods, I would be able to explain this matter to the Blessed One for an entire day using various words and various methods; even if [he were to ask] for an entire night... [and so on].
Even for a single day and night, may the Blessed One [instruct me]...
even for two days and nights, may the Blessed One [instruct me]...
even for three...
four … five … six …

if I were to ask Sāriputta about this matter for an entire day using various terms and various methods,

4. Kaḷārakhattiyavagga Ñāṇavatthusutta At Sāvatthī. …
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you forty-four bases of knowledge.
Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, what are the forty-four bases of knowledge?
Knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death, knowledge of the cessation of aging-and-death, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of aging-and-death;”
Knowledge of birth, knowledge of the origin of birth, knowledge of the cessation of birth, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of birth;
knowledge of existence, knowledge of the origin of existence, knowledge of the cessation of existence, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of existence;
knowledge of clinging, knowledge of the origin of clinging, knowledge of the cessation of clinging, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of clinging.
Knowledge of craving, knowledge of the origin of craving, knowledge of the cessation of craving, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of craving;
knowledge of feeling, knowledge of the origin of feeling, knowledge of the cessation of feeling, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of feeling;
knowledge of contact … [and so forth] …
Knowledge of the six sense bases… knowledge of name-and-form… knowledge of consciousness…

Knowledge of volitional formations, knowledge of the origin of volitional formations, knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations, and knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
These, monks, are called the forty-four bases of knowledge.
And what, monks, is aging-and-death?
Whatever aging, decrepitude, brokenness, graying, wrinkling, and decline of the life-force occurs among various beings in their respective classes of beings;
the ripening of the faculties—this is called aging.

Whatever passing away, perishing, dissolution, disappearance, death, dying, completion of time, breaking up of the aggregates, and casting off of the body occurs among various beings from their respective classes of beings—this is called death.
This is called death.
Thus, this aging and this death—
this, monks, is called aging-and-death.
With the arising of birth, there is the arising of aging and death;
with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of aging and death, namely: [the rest of the eight factors].
Right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.

When, monks, a noble disciple understands aging-and-death in this way, understands the origin of aging-and-death in this way, understands the cessation of aging-and-death in this way, and understands the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death in this way—
He understands this; this is his knowledge regarding the Dhamma.
By means of this Dhamma—which is seen, known, timeless, attained, and fully penetrated—he draws the conclusion concerning the past and the future:
"Whatever recluses or brahmins in the past have directly realized aging-and-death and the origin of aging-and-death..."

They have directly known aging and death; they have directly known the cessation of aging and death; they have directly known the path leading to the cessation of aging and death—all of them have directly known it in exactly this way, just as I do now.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future time will directly know aging and death, and the origin of aging and death...
"They will directly know aging and death; they will directly know the cessation of aging and death;
they will directly know the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death—all these will directly know it in exactly the same way as I do now.
This is his knowledge by inference.
When, monks, these two kinds of knowledge are purified and cleansed for a noble disciple—
knowledge of the Dhamma and subsequent knowledge—
then, monks, this noble disciple is said to be "one accomplished in view" and also "one accomplished in vision."
"Thus he has come to this true Dhamma; thus he sees this true Dhamma; thus he is endowed with the knowledge of one in training;
thus he is endowed with the clear vision of one in training; thus he has entered the stream of the Dhamma; thus he is a noble one of penetrative wisdom;
thus he stands knocking at the door of the Deathless."
And what, monks, is birth?
And what, monks, is existence?
And what, monks, is clinging?
And what, bhikkhus, is craving?
And what, bhikkhus, is feeling?
And what, bhikkhus, is contact?
And what, monks, is the sixfold base?
… And what, monks, is name-and-form?
… And what, monks, is consciousness? …
And what, monks, are volitional formations?
There are these three, monks, that are volitional formations:
the bodily volitional formation, the verbal volitional formation, and the mental volitional formation.
These, monks, are called volitional formations.
With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of volitional formations;
with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
When, monks, a noble disciple understands volitional formations in this way, and understands the origin of volitional formations in this way, [he is called a noble disciple who has understood.]
Thus he understands the cessation of volitional formations; thus he understands the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations. This is his knowledge regarding phenomena (*dhamme ñāṇa*).
By means of this Dhamma—seen, known, timeless, attained, and fathomed—he draws the inference concerning the past and the future.
Whatever recluses or brahmins in the past have directly known volitional formations and the arising of volitional formations...

They have directly known formations; they have directly known the cessation of formations; they have directly known the path leading to the cessation of formations—all of them have directly known exactly as I do now.
And whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will directly know formations and the origination of formations...
They will directly know the cessation of formations; they will directly know the path leading to the cessation of formations—all these will directly know it in exactly the same way as I do now.
This is his knowledge by inference.
“Bhikkhus, when these two kinds of knowledge of a noble disciple are purified and cleansed—
knowledge of the Dhamma and subsequent knowledge—
this noble disciple is called one who is accomplished in view, and also one who is accomplished in vision.”
"Thus he has come to this true Dhamma; thus he sees this true Dhamma; thus he is endowed with the knowledge of one in training;
thus he is endowed with the clear vision of one in training; thus he has entered the stream of the Dhamma; thus he is a noble one of penetrative wisdom;
thus he stands knocking at the door of the Deathless."

The Discourse on the Basis for the Second Knowledge.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Monks, I will teach you seventy-seven bases for knowledge.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, what are the seventy-seven bases of knowledge?
The knowledge that ‘with birth as condition there is aging-and-death’;
the knowledge that ‘in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death’;”
There is the knowledge: "In the past time too, with birth as condition, there was aging-and-death"; the knowledge: "If there were no birth, there would be no aging-and-death"; the knowledge:
"In the future time too, with birth as condition, there will be aging-and-death"; the knowledge: "If there were no birth, there would be no aging-and-death";
and the knowledge that even this knowledge of the stability of phenomena is itself subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.
Knowledge that "with existence as condition, birth [comes to be]"; ...
knowledge that "with clinging as condition, existence [comes to be]";
... knowledge that "with craving as condition, clinging [comes to be]".
Knowledge that "with feeling as condition, craving arises" ...
knowledge that "with contact as condition, feeling arises" ...
knowledge that "with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises" ...
Knowledge that "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [arise]";
knowledge that "with consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises]";
knowledge that "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness [arises]";
The knowledge that "with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations," the knowledge that "in the absence of ignorance there are no volitional formations";
the knowledge that "in the past period too, with ignorance as condition there were volitional formations," the knowledge that "in the absence of ignorance there were no volitional formations";

the knowledge that "in the future period too, with ignorance as condition there will be volitional formations," the knowledge that "in the absence of ignorance there will be no volitional formations."
“Furthermore, the knowledge that even this knowledge of the stability of phenomena is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away,
and subject to cessation— these, monks, are called the seventy-seven bases of knowledge.

Kaḷārakhattiya-vagga Avijjā-paccaya-sutta: The Conditionality of Ignorance At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, ignorance is the forerunner in the arising of unwholesome states; it arises first, and subsequently unwholesome states arise. And what, bhikkhus, is that ignorance? It is the lack of knowledge regarding suffering, the lack of knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, the lack of knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and the lack of knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called ignorance. “And what, bhikkhus, are the unwholesome states? They are: covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. These are called unwholesome states. Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, these unwholesome states come to be. “Bhikkhus, knowledge is the forerunner in the arising of wholesome states; it arises first, and subsequently wholesome states arise. And what, bhikkhus, is that knowledge? It is the knowledge regarding suffering, the knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, the knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and the knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called knowledge. “And what, bhikkhus, are the wholesome states? They are: non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view. These are called wholesome states. Thus, bhikkhus, with knowledge as condition, these wholesome states come to be.”

whether it be "the soul is the same as the body" or "the soul is one thing and the body another," bhikkhu— when such a view exists, there is no living of the holy life. When such a view exists, bhikkhu, there is no living of the holy life.

The Fifth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.36 (SN 12.36, PTS SN ii 63) 4. The Chapter on the Warrior Kaḷāra The Discourse on the Warrior Kaḷāra Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a warrior named Kaḷāra, a khattiya, who had been brought up since childhood, well-trained, skilled, and experienced in the arts of warfare. He would mount a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses that were well-bred, swift, and well-trained, with a banner raised high. He would go out to the battlefield surrounded by a retinue of warriors. Then, having gone out to the battlefield, he would see his own army arrayed and the enemy army arrayed. Seeing them, he would think: ‘This is my own army; this is the enemy army. These are my own warriors; these are the enemy warriors. These are my own charioteers; these are the enemy charioteers. These are my own horses; these are the enemy horses. Having seen this, he would think: ‘My own army is strong and the enemy army is weak; my own army is large and the enemy army is small; my own army is well-prepared and the enemy army is ill-prepared; my own army is well-armed and the enemy army is poorly armed; my own army is well-led and the enemy army is ill-led. Having reflected thus, he would think: ‘I am not equal to engaging in battle with the enemy army. It would be better for me to retreat. And so he would retreat. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a warrior named Kaḷāra, a khattiya, who had been brought up since childhood, well-trained, skilled, and experienced in the arts of warfare. He would mount a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses that were well-bred, swift, and well-trained, with a banner raised high. He would go out to the battlefield surrounded by a retinue of warriors. Then, having gone out to the battlefield, he would see his own army arrayed and the enemy army arrayed. Seeing them, he would think: ‘This is my own army; this is the enemy army. These are my own warriors; these are the enemy warriors. These are my own charioteers; these are the enemy charioteers. These are my own horses; these are the enemy horses. Having seen this, he would think: ‘My own army is strong and the enemy army is weak; my own army is large and the enemy army is small; my own army is well-prepared and the enemy army is ill-prepared; my own army is well-armed and the enemy army is poorly armed; my own army is well-led and the enemy army is ill-led. Having reflected thus, he would think: ‘I am equal to engaging in battle with the enemy army. I shall engage them. And so he would engage them.

“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a warrior named Kaḷāra, a khattiya, who had been brought up since childhood, well-trained, skilled, and experienced in the arts of warfare. He would mount a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses that were well-bred, swift, and well-trained, with a banner raised high. He would go out to the battlefield surrounded by a retinue of warriors. Then, having gone out to the battlefield, he would see his own army arrayed and the enemy army arrayed. Seeing them, he would think: ‘This is my own army; this is the enemy army. These are my own warriors; these are the enemy warriors. These are my own charioteers; these are the enemy charioteers. These are my own horses; these are the enemy horses. Having seen this, he would think: ‘My own army is strong and the enemy army is weak; my own army is large and the enemy army is small; my own army is well-prepared and the enemy army is ill-prepared; my own army is well-armed and the enemy army is poorly armed; my own army is well-led and the enemy army is ill-led. Having reflected thus, he would think: ‘I am superior to engaging in battle with the enemy army. I shall engage them and conquer them. And so he would engage them and conquer them. “Bhikkhus, just as that warrior named Kaḷāra, a khattiya, would reflect before engaging in battle, so too, bhikkhus, a noble disciple reflects before engaging in the battle of the Dhamma. He reflects thus: ‘Are there within me any underlying tendencies of sensual lust, or underlying tendencies of aversion, or underlying tendencies of ignorance, which, being unabandoned, might lead to my downfall? If, upon reflection, he knows:

‘There are within me no underlying tendencies of sensual lust, no underlying tendencies of aversion, and no underlying tendencies of ignorance, which, being unabandoned, might lead to my downfall,’ then he dwells in that state, mindful and clearly comprehending, having attained security from bondage. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘There are within me underlying tendencies of sensual lust, underlying tendencies of aversion, and underlying tendencies of ignorance, which, being unabandoned, might lead to my downfall,’ then he exerts himself to abandon those underlying tendencies. “Bhikkhus, just as that warrior named Kaḷāra, a khattiya, would reflect before engaging in battle, so too, bhikkhus, a noble disciple reflects before engaging in the battle of the Dhamma. He reflects thus: ‘Am I one who acts with full awareness when going forward and returning; when looking ahead and looking aside; when drawing in and extending the limbs; when wearing the robes and carrying the bowl; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when defecating and urinating; when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and remaining silent? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I am one who acts with full awareness in all these things,’ then he dwells in that state, mindful and clearly comprehending, having attained security from bondage. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I am not one who acts with full awareness in all these things,’ then he exerts himself to practice full awareness. “Bhikkhus, just as that warrior named Kaḷāra, a khattiya, would reflect before engaging in battle, so too, bhikkhus, a noble disciple reflects before engaging in the battle of the Dhamma. He reflects thus: ‘Do I possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha: “The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One”? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha,’ then he dwells in that state, mindful and clearly comprehending, having attained security from bondage. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I do not possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha,’ then he exerts himself to attain unwavering confidence in the Buddha. He reflects thus: ‘Do I possess unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: “The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise”? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I possess unwavering confidence in the Dhamma,’ then he dwells in that state, mindful and clearly comprehending, having attained security from bondage. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I do not possess unwavering confidence in the Dhamma,’ then he exerts himself to attain unwavering confidence in the Dhamma. He reflects thus: ‘Do I possess unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world”? If, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I possess unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha,’ then he dwells in that state, mindful and clearly comprehending, having attained security from bondage. But if, upon reflection, he knows: ‘I do not possess unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha,’ then he exerts himself to attain unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha. “Bhikkhus, just as that warrior named Kaḷāra, a khattiya, would reflect before engaging in battle, so too, bhikkhus, a noble disciple reflects before engaging in the battle of the Dhamma.
The Second Discourse on the Condition of Ignorance.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be.”
“With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises …pe… such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
Or, monks, whoever should say: ‘What is aging-and-death, and for whom is there this aging-and-death?’”
“Bhikkhus, if anyone were to say, ‘Aging-and-death is one thing, and this aging-and-death is another,’ both of these refer to the same thing;
only the phrasing is different.
Or, bhikkhus, if the view ‘The soul is the same as the body’ exists, there is no living of the holy life.”
“‘The soul is one thing and the body another,’ monks—if such a view exists, there is no living of the holy life.
Without approaching either of these two extremes, monks, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way:
‘With birth as condition, aging and death come to be.’”
What is birth? ... What is existence?
... What is clinging?
What is craving?
… What is feeling?
… What is contact? …
What is the sixfold sense base?
… What is name-and-form?
… What is consciousness?
“Monks, whether one should say, ‘What are these volitional formations? And for whom are these volitional formations?
or whether one should say, ‘The volitional formations are one thing, and these volitional formations belong to another,’ both of these mean the same thing;
only the phrasing is different.”
“Bhikkhus, when there is the view ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ the living of the holy life does not occur;
or when there is the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ the living of the holy life does not occur.
Without veering toward either of these two extremes, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way:”
‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, monks, whatever those writhings, wrigglings, and quiverings of his may be—
whether it be the thought, ‘What is aging-and-death, and for whom is this aging-and-death?’, or ‘Aging-and-death is one thing, and for another...’— [they all cease].
Or “this is aging-and-death,” or “the soul is the same as the body,” or “the soul is one thing and the body another.
All these views of his have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
It is, monks, through the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance that whatever such writhings, wrigglings, and wrappings there may be [on the part of others]... [cease].
What is birth? ... What is existence?
... What is clinging?
What is craving?
… What is feeling?
… What is contact? …
What is the sixfold base?
… What is name-and-form?
… What is consciousness?

“Whether it be: ‘What are these volitional formations? And for whom do these volitional formations belong? or ‘The volitional formations are one thing, and for another person these volitional formations belong’;

or ‘That which is the soul is the body,’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body is another’—all such views have been abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
Thus ends the sixth [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.37 (SN 12.37, PTS SN ii 64) 4. Kaḷārakhattiyavagga Natumhasutta “Bhikkhus, it is not yours; abandon it. When abandoned, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? The eye is not yours: abandon it. When abandoned, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. The ear is not yours... The nose is not yours... The tongue is not yours... The body is not yours... The mind is not yours: abandon it. When abandoned, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, who is the owner of the eye? Who is the owner of the ear? Who is the owner of the nose? Who is the owner of the tongue? Who is the owner of the body? Who is the owner of the mind? “Ānanda, the eye is not yours, nor is it anyone else’s. It is simply a phenomenon conditioned by contact. The ear is not yours, nor is it anyone else’s. It is simply a phenomenon conditioned by contact. The nose is not yours, nor is it anyone else’s. It is simply a phenomenon conditioned by contact. The tongue is not yours, nor is it anyone else’s. It is simply a phenomenon conditioned by contact. The body is not yours, nor is it anyone else’s. It is simply a phenomenon conditioned by contact. The mind is not yours, nor is it anyone else’s. It is simply a phenomenon conditioned by contact. “Whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or pondered by the intellect—when it is not yours, abandon it. When abandoned, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went into his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend! those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, suppose a man were to come along carrying a lamp. He would see the forms illuminated by its light. Even so, friends, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways, as he who has knowledge, as he who has vision, as he who has understanding, as he who has awakening, as he who has arrived at the supreme goal, as the knower of worlds, as the incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, as the teacher of gods and humans, as the Buddha, as the Blessed One. “The eye, friends, is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not mine; this is not my self; this is not what I am. The ear is impermanent... The nose is impermanent... The tongue is impermanent... The body is impermanent... The mind is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not mine; this is not my self; this is not what I am. “Seeing thus, friends, the instructed noble disciple experiences revulsion toward the eye, revulsion toward the ear, revulsion toward the nose, revulsion toward the tongue, revulsion toward the body, revulsion toward the mind. Experiencing revulsion, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion [his mind] is liberated. When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Venerable Ānanda’s words. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Staying at Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One said]: "Monks, this body is not yours, nor does it belong to others.
Monks, this should be seen as old karma—wrought, volitionally produced, and to be experienced."
In this regard, monks, the learned noble disciple carefully and thoroughly attends to dependent origination thus:
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say:"

Kaḷārakhattiya-vagga (The Chapter on Kaḷārakhattiya)
The Discourse on Volition. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was dwelling there.
“Monks, whatever one intends, whatever one plans, and whatever one has a latent tendency toward—that becomes an object for the persistence of consciousness.”
When there is an object, there is a foundation for consciousness.
When consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be in the future.
In this way there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
But if, monks, one does not intend and does not plan, yet still has underlying tendencies, that becomes a basis for the stationing of consciousness.
When there is a basis, there is a support for the stationing of consciousness.
When consciousness is established and grows, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there come to be birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair in the future.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But when, monks, one neither intends, nor plans, nor has underlying tendencies, this does not become an object for the persistence of consciousness.
When there is no object, there is no foundation for consciousness.
When consciousness is unestablished and does not grow, there is no production of renewed existence in the future.
When there is no production of renewed existence in the future, then birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease in the future.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Thus ends the eighth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.39 (SN 12.39, PTS SN ii 66) 4. Kaḷārakhattiya-vagga Second Discourse on Volition “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you volition and the origin of volition. Listen and attend closely; I will speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “And what, bhikkhus, is volition? It is the mental volitional formation that arises dependent on the mind. This, bhikkhus, is called volition. “And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of volition? Dependent on the mind, there arises contact; dependent on contact, feeling; dependent on feeling, craving; dependent on craving, clinging; dependent on clinging, existence; dependent on existence, birth; dependent on birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of volition. “And how, bhikkhus, is there a cessation of volition? With the cessation of the mind comes the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus there is a cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of volition.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.40 (SN 12.40, PTS SN ii 66) 4.

The Third Discourse on Volition.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Monks, whatever one intends, whatever one plans, and whatever one has a latent tendency toward—that becomes an object for the persistence of consciousness.”
When there is an object, there is a support for consciousness.
When consciousness is supported and has grown, there is inclination.
When there is inclination, there is coming and going.
When there is coming and going, there is passing away and rebirth.
When there is passing away and rebirth, there come to be birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair in the future.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
If, monks, one does not intend and does not plan, but still has a latent tendency, this becomes a basis for the persistence of consciousness.
When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness.
When consciousness is supported and has grown, there is a leaning toward rebirth.
When there is bending, there is coming and going.
When there is coming and going, there is passing away and rebirth.
When there is passing away and rebirth, there come to be birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair in the future.
"Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, when five fears and enmities have been stilled for a noble disciple,
when he is endowed with the four factors of stream-entry, and when the noble method has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom,
he could, if he so desired, declare of himself:”

“I have exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal womb; I have exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower realms. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.
What five fears and enmities have been stilled?
Householder, whatever fear and enmity one who destroys living beings generates on account of that destruction of living beings—even in this very life—[that has been stilled].
It produces fear and enmity pertaining to future lives, and one experiences mental pain and dejection;
for one who abstains from taking life, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
Householder, when one who takes what is not given, on account of taking what is not given, produces fear and enmity pertaining to the present life... [and so forth].
One produces fear and enmity pertaining to future lives, and one experiences mental pain and grief;
for one who abstains from taking what is not given, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
Furthermore, householder, for one who engages in sexual misconduct regarding sensual pleasures, there arises fear pertaining to the present life on account of that sexual misconduct.
One engenders enmity; one engenders enmity that leads to fear in future lives; one experiences mental pain and dejection.
For one who abstains from sexual misconduct, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
Furthermore, householder, a speaker of falsehood engenders enmity and fear pertaining to the present life because of that falsehood.
One produces fear and enmity pertaining to future lives, and one experiences mental pain and grief;
for one who abstains from false speech, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.

Householder, as for the one who indulges in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which cause negligence, on account of such indulgence in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which cause negligence, there arises even in this present life...
It produces fear and enmity; it produces fear and enmity pertaining to the future life;
and one experiences mental pain and grief. For one who abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
These five fears and enmities have been stilled.
With which four factors of stream-entry is he endowed?
Here, householder, the noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha: [text continues]

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma:
‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves.’
He is endowed with verified confidence in the Saṅgha:
"The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically,
the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing correctly— that is to say, the four [pairs of persons]."

‘There are these eight pairs of persons, these twenty-four individual persons; this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples that is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
He is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
He is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry.
And what is the noble method that has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom?
Here, householder, the noble disciple attends thoroughly and wisely to dependent origination itself:
"Thus, when this exists, that comes to be; from the non-existence of this, that does not come to be.
With the arising of this, that arises; with the cessation of this, that ceases.
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise."
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises ...
and so on ... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations;
With the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
This noble method of his has been well seen and well penetrated by means of wisdom.
Householder, when these five fears and enmities have been stilled for a noble disciple,

Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta The Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Friend Sāriputta, it is said, ‘an elephant’s footprint, an elephant’s footprint. In what way, friend, is there the expression ‘an elephant’s footprint’? (1) “Friends, suppose a cowherd’s boy were to collect all the footprints made by the hoofprints of cattle in the track of a herd of cattle and say: ‘These are the largest footprints,’ he would be speaking correctly, not falsely. Why is that? Because the elephant’s footprint is the greatest of all the footprints made by the hoofprints of cattle in the track of a herd of cattle. So too, friends, among the states conducive to direct knowledge, the state of the noble disciple who has entered the stream is the greatest. (2) “Suppose, friends, a cowherd’s boy were to collect all the water found in puddles in the track of a herd of cattle and say: ‘This is the greatest body of water,’ he would be speaking correctly, not falsely. with clinging as condition, existence arises.

with feeling as condition, there is craving.

"To say, 'Everything exists,' Brahmin, is the oldest form of Lokāyata."
“But, Master Gotama, is it that everything does not exist?
“‘Everything does not exist,’ Brahmin, is the second form of Lokāyata.
“But, Master Gotama, is everything a single unity?”
“‘All is one,’ brahmin, is the third worldly doctrine.
“But what, Master Gotama, is ‘all is manifold’?
“‘All is manifold,’ brahmin, is the fourth worldly doctrine.”
“Brahmin, without approaching either of these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way:
‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises... [and so on].
Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness... [and so on]...
“Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
When this was said, the Lokāyata brahmin said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! … [as before] …”
“From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, we go for refuge.
Thus [ends] the eighth.

At Sāvatthī he was staying.
“Bhikkhus, it does not occur to the learned noble disciple thus:
‘What now exists when what exists? From the arising of what does what arise?’”
When what exists are volitional formations? When what exists is consciousness? When what exists are name-and-form?
When what exists are the six sense bases? When what exists is contact? When what exists is feeling?
When what exists is craving? When what exists is clinging? When what exists is existence? When what exists is birth?
‘When what exists does aging-and-death come to be?
Then, monks, for the well-taught noble disciple, there comes to be knowledge independent of others:
‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.’”
When ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be;
when volitional formations exist, consciousness comes to be;
when consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be.
When name-and-form exists, the six sense bases come to be;
when the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be;
when contact exists, feeling comes to be.
When there is feeling, craving arises;
when there is craving, clinging arises;
when there is clinging, existence arises.
"When there is existence, birth comes to be;
when there is birth, aging and death come to be.
He understands thus:
‘In this way, this world arises.
Monks, it does not occur to the learned noble disciple:
‘What now—’
When what is absent, what does not come to be? With the cessation of what, what ceases?
When what is absent, volitional formations do not come to be? When what is absent, consciousness does not come to be? When what is absent, name-and-form does not come to be?
When what is absent, the six sense bases do not come to be? When what is absent, contact does not come to be? When what is absent...
‘When there is no feeling, what being absent does craving not come to be? When what is absent does clinging not come to be?
When what is absent does existence not come to be? When what is absent does birth not come to be? When what is absent do aging and death not come to be?
Then, monks, for the well-taught noble disciple, there arises here knowledge independent of others:
‘When this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases.
When ignorance is not, volitional formations are not;
when volitional formations are not, consciousness is not.’
When consciousness is absent, name-and-form does not come to be;
when name-and-form is absent, the six sense bases do not come to be...
[and so on] ...when becoming is absent, birth does not come to be.
‘Birth does not exist… when birth is absent, aging and death do not exist.
He understands thus:

When there is no feeling, in the absence of what does craving not come to be?
… [and so on] … clinging … becoming …
‘When what does not exist is there no aging and death? Then, monks,

accomplished in vision, one who has arrived at this true Dhamma, one who sees this true Dhamma, one who possesses the knowledge of a trainee,

The Chapter on Suffering (Dukkhavagga)
The Discourse on Investigation.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus.
"Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“To what extent, monks, should a monk, when investigating thoroughly, investigate for the sake of the complete and total destruction of suffering?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be well, indeed…”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One himself explain the meaning of this statement; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, monks, a monk, investigating thoroughly, investigates thus:
‘Whatever various and manifold kinds of suffering arise in the world, such as aging and death—’”
‘What now is this suffering: what is its source, what is its origin, from what is it born?
When what exists does aging-and-death come to be; when what does not exist does aging-and-death not come to be?
As he investigates, he understands thus:
‘Whatever various kinds of suffering arise in the world—aging and death—this suffering has birth as its source, birth as its origin, is born of birth, and has birth as its provenance.
When there is birth, aging and death come to be; when there is no birth, aging and death do not come to be.
Thus he understands aging and death, he understands the origin of aging and death, and he understands the cessation of aging and death.
And he understands that practice which leads to the cessation of aging and death, and he practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma.
This, monks, is called a monk who is practicing entirely for the right destruction of suffering, for the cessation of aging and death.
Furthermore, examining further, he examines:
‘What is the source of this birth? What is its origin? From what is it born? From what does it arise? When what exists does birth come to be?
When what does not exist does birth not come to be? Examining this, he understands thus:

‘Birth has existence as its source, existence as its origin; it is born from existence, it arises from existence. When there is existence, birth comes to be; when there is no existence, birth does not come to be.’”
"When there is existence, birth comes to be; when there is no existence, birth does not come to be.

He understands birth, he understands the origin of birth, he understands the cessation of birth, and he understands the practice that leads to the cessation of birth; and he practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma.
This, monks, is called a monk who is practicing for the complete destruction of suffering through the cessation of birth.
Then, further investigating, he investigates:
“What is the source of this becoming?
… What is the source of this clinging?”
But what is this craving rooted in?
... Feeling ...
Contact ...
But what is the source of these six sense bases?
… What is the source of this name-and-form?
… What is the source of this consciousness? …
"But what is the source of these volitional formations? What is their origin? From what are they born? From what do they arise?
When what exists do volitional formations come to be? When what does not exist do volitional formations not come to be?
As he investigates, he understands thus:
“Volitional formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and ignorance as their cause.
When there is ignorance, volitional formations come to be; when there is no ignorance, volitional formations do not come to be.
Thus he understands volitional formations, he understands the origin of volitional formations, and he understands the cessation of volitional formations.
And he understands that path which leads to the cessation of volitional formations and is conducive to it; he practices accordingly and lives in accordance with the Dhamma.
This, monks, is called a monk who is practicing for the complete and right destruction of suffering, for the cessation of volitional formations.
Monks, when a person immersed in ignorance performs a meritorious volitional formation, his consciousness becomes destined for merit.
If one performs a meritorious volitional formation, consciousness becomes associated with merit. If one performs a demeritorious volitional formation, consciousness becomes associated with demerit.
If one performs an imperturbable volitional formation, consciousness becomes associated with the imperturbable.
But when, monks, a monk has abandoned ignorance and true knowledge has arisen, through the fading away of ignorance...
With the arising of true knowledge, one neither forms a volitional formation of merit, nor forms a volitional formation of demerit,
nor forms a volitional formation of the imperturbable.
Not forming, not intending, one does not cling to anything in the world.
Not grasping, one does not tremble; not trembling, one attains nibbāna right here and now.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
When such a person experiences a pleasant feeling, they understand it as impermanent, they understand it as unclung-to, and they understand it as unenjoyed.
If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: "It is impermanent"; he understands: "It is not clung to"; he understands: "It is not rejoiced in.
If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: "It is impermanent"; he understands: "It is not clung to"; he understands: "It is not rejoiced in.
If he feels a pleasant feeling, being detached, he feels it.
If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached;
if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.

When feeling a feeling that ends with the body, he understands: "I feel a feeling that ends with the body"; when feeling a feeling that ends with life, he understands: "I feel a feeling that ends with life."
He understands: "With the breakup of the body, after the exhaustion of life, all that is felt here, no longer being delighted in, will become cool; only the physical remains will persist.
Monks, it is just as if a man were to take a hot pot out of a kiln and set it down on a level patch of ground.
There, whatever heat there was would be extinguished right then and there, while the shards would remain behind.
In the same way, monks, when a monk experiences a feeling that ends with the body, he understands: "I experience a feeling that ends with the body";
when he experiences a feeling that ends with life, he understands: "I experience a feeling that ends with life."
“With the breakup of the body, after the exhaustion of life, he understands: ‘Right here all that is felt, being no longer delighted in, will become cool;
only the physical remains will persist.

What do you think, bhikkhus, would a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed still perform a volitional formation of merit, or a volitional formation of demerit, or a volitional formation of the imperturbable?”
“No, venerable sir.
“But if there were absolutely no volitional formations, with the cessation of volitional formations, would consciousness be discerned?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Furthermore, if consciousness were entirely absent, with the cessation of consciousness, would name-and-form be discerned?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“Furthermore, if name-and-form were entirely absent, with the cessation of name-and-form, would the six sense bases be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“But if there were absolutely no six sense bases, with the cessation of the six sense bases, would contact be discerned?
“No, venerable sir.”
“But if, entirely, there were no contact, with the cessation of contact, would feeling be discerned?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“But if, entirely, there were no feeling, with the cessation of feeling, would craving be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“But if there were absolutely no craving, with the cessation of craving, would clinging be discerned?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Furthermore, when there is no clinging at all, with the cessation of clinging, would existence be discerned?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
“Furthermore, when there is no existence at all, with the cessation of existence, would birth be discerned?”
“No, venerable sir.
“But when there is no birth at all, with the cessation of birth, would aging-and-death be discerned?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Excellent, excellent, monks! It is so, monks; it is not otherwise.
Believe me in this, monks, resolve upon it, and be free from doubt and free from uncertainty here:
‘This indeed is the end of suffering.’”
First.

The Chapter on Suffering (Dukkhavagga)
The Discourse on Clinging. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that can be clung to, craving increases.”
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
Monks, it is just as if a great mass of fire were to burn from ten loads of wood, or twenty loads of wood, or thirty loads of wood, or forty loads of wood.
In that case, monks, if from time to time a man were to throw dry grass into it, dry cow dung into it, and dry wood into it, then, monks,
that great mass of fire, with that as its fuel and that as its support, would burn for a long, extended period. In the same way, monks,
craving increases for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that lead to grasping.
With craving as condition, clinging arises...
thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
For one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that provoke clinging, monks, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence;
with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
With the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Just as, monks, a great mass of fire might burn from ten, twenty, thirty, or forty loads of wood;
In that case, monks, if a man were not from time to time to throw dry grass into it, nor throw dry cow dung into it, nor throw dry wood into it,
then, monks, that great mass of fire, through the exhaustion of its previous fuel and the non-supply of any other, would go out for lack of sustenance. In the same way, monks,
for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that can be clung to, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging … [and so on] … such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Thus ends the second [discourse].

At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, craving increases.
With craving as condition, there is clinging.”
With clinging as condition, existence comes to be;
with existence as condition, birth;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.

Just as, monks, an oil lamp might burn in dependence on oil and a wick;

With clinging as condition, existence comes to be;
with existence as condition, birth;

with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;

and a man were neither to pour oil into it from time to time nor to replace the wick.
