"Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12.57 (SN 12.57, PTS SN ii 89).
6. The Chapter on Suffering:
The Discourse on the Young Tree.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, craving increases.
With craving as condition,
there is clinging … [and so on] … such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.”
“Just as if, monks, there were a young tree,
and a man would from time to time rub its roots, from time to time give it soil, and from time to time give it water.
In this way, monks, that young tree— being nourished by that and taking up that sustenance— would attain growth, increase, and abundance.”
In the same way, monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that fetter, craving increases.
With craving as condition, there is clinging...
and so on... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that fetter, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging … [and so on] … such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
“Just as if, monks, there were a young tree,
and then a man would come along carrying a hoe and a basket...
[and so on] ...or he would carry it away in the swift current of a river.”
"In this way, monks, that young tree would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and no longer subject to future arising.
Even so, monks, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that fetter, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging... [and so on]..."
"Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
The seventh [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12.58. (SN 12.58, PTS SN ii 90)
6. The Chapter on Suffering:
Discourse on Name-and-Form.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that fetter, there is the descent of name-and-form.
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise … [and so on] … such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.”
“Just as, monks, there might be a great tree:
whatever roots of it go downward and whatever go sideways, they all carry nourishment upward.
For in this way, monks, that great tree—having that as its nutriment and that as its support—might endure for a very long time.”
In the same way, monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that fetter, there is a descent of name-and-form...
[as before] ... For one who dwells contemplating danger in phenomena that fetter, monks, there is no descent of name-and-form.
With the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases... [as before] ...
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Just as if, monks, there were a great tree, and then a man were to come along carrying a spade and a basket... [and so on].
It is of a nature not to arise again in the future.
In the same way, monks, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that fetter, there is no descent of name-and-form.
With the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases... [and so on]...
"Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
The eighth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.59 (SN 12.59, PTS SN ii 91).
6. The Chapter on Suffering:
The Discourse on Consciousness. At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was staying.
“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that fetter, there is a descent of consciousness.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form [arises] …pe… such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
“Just as, monks, there is a great tree:
whatever its roots...
[as above] ...even so, monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that lead to fetters, there occurs the descent of consciousness... [as above] ...”
“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that fetter, there is no descent of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form … [and so on] … such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
“Just as if, monks, there were a great tree,
and then a man were to come along carrying a spade and a basket...
[and so on] ...it would be of a nature not to arise again in the future.”
“In the same way, monks, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that fetter, there is no descent of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form...
[as before] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
The Ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.60 (SN 12.60, PTS SN ii 92) 6.
The Chapter on Suffering (Dukkhavagga)
The Nidāna Sutta On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!
How profound this dependent origination is, venerable sir, and how profound it appears; yet to me it seems as clear as something plain on the palm of one’s hand.
“Do not say that, Ānanda! Do not say that, Ānanda!”
"Ānanda, this dependent origination is deep and appears deep.

It is through not awakening to and not penetrating this Dhamma, Ānanda, that this generation has become like a tangled skein, like a knotted ball of thread, like matted rushes and reeds, and does not transcend states of deprivation, ill destiny, and ruin, nor pass beyond the cycle of saṃsāra.
For one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena conducive to clinging, Ānanda, craving increases."
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises;
with existence as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
It is just like a great tree, Ānanda.
Whatever roots of his go downward and whatever go sideways, they all carry nourishment upward.
In this way, Ānanda, that great tree—having that as its nutriment and that as its support—might endure for a long time.
Even so, Ānanda, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that lead to clinging, craving increases.
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises...
and so on... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
Ānanda, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in phenomena that are subject to clinging, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence … [and so on] …
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
It is just as if, Ānanda, there were a great tree,
and then a man were to come along carrying a spade and a basket.
Suppose one were to cut that tree at its root, and having cut it at the root, were to dig it up; having dug it up, one would extract the roots, even down to the fibers as fine as a hair.
One would then cut that tree into pieces, and having cut it into pieces, were to split them apart.
Having split it into pieces, one would reduce it to fragments; having reduced it to fragments, one would dry it in the wind and sun;
having dried it in the wind and sun, one would burn it with fire; having burned it with fire, one would reduce it to ashes;
having reduced it to ashes, one would scatter the ashes in a great wind or carry them away in a swift-flowing river.
In this way, Ānanda, that great tree would be cut off at the root, made like the stump of a palm tree, rendered non-existent, and subject to the state of not arising again in the future.
Even so, Ānanda, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that lead to clinging, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging.
With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases;
with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Tenth. The sixth chapter on Suffering is concluded.
Its summary verse: Investigation,
clinging, and the two fetters.
Two are spoken of by means of the great tree,
and the seventh by the young tree;
[the remaining two are] name-and-form and consciousness.
"And you [should know] them by way of their causal origin.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12.61 (SN 12.61, PTS SN ii 94), 7. Mahāvagga.
The Discourse on the Unlearned:
Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. …
“Bhikkhus, an uninstructed worldling might become disenchanted with, dispassionate toward, and liberated from this body composed of the four great elements.
Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the accumulation and the depletion of this body composed of the four great elements, as well as its acquisition and its laying down, are seen.”
Therefore, in that regard, the uninstructed worldling might become disenchanted, might become dispassionate, and might be liberated.

But as for this which is called "mind," or "intellect," or "consciousness"—in that regard, the uninstructed worldling is not capable of becoming disenchanted, not capable of becoming dispassionate, and not capable of being liberated. Why is that?
For a long time, monks, this has been clung to, cherished as "mine," and grasped by the uninstructed worldling as:
"This is mine, this am I, this is my self.
Therefore, regarding that, the uninstructed worldling is not capable of becoming disenchanted, not capable of dispassion, and not capable of liberation.
“Bhikkhus, it would be better for an uninstructed worldling to regard this body composed of the four great elements as self rather than the mind.
Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, this body composed of the four great elements can be seen to persist for one year, even two years.”
Remaining for three years, remaining for four years, remaining for five years, remaining for ten years,
remaining for twenty years, remaining for thirty years,
remaining for forty years, remaining for fifty years, [or] even for a hundred years.
"Remaining, remaining even more;
yet, monks, that which is called 'mind,' or 'intellect,' or 'consciousness,' arises as one thing and ceases as another, both by night and by day.
Just as a monkey, monks, wandering through a forest thicket, grasps a branch, lets go of it, and grasps another, letting go of that and grasping yet another."
In the same way, monks, that which is called ‘mind’ (citta), or ‘intellect’ (mano), or ‘consciousness’ (viññāṇa), arises as one thing and ceases as another during the night and the day.
In this regard, monks, the well-taught noble disciple carefully and thoroughly attends to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) thus:
‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.’
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases—namely:
with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises …pe….
Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness... [and so on]...
"Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated."
“He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus it was said. First.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 12.62. (SN 12.62, PTS SN ii 95)
7. Mahāvagga: The Second Discourse on the Unlearned.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling might grow disenchanted with this body composed of the four great elements, might become dispassionate toward it, and might be liberated from it.
Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the accumulation and the depletion of this body composed of the four great elements, as well as its acquisition and its casting off, are seen.”
Therefore, in that regard, the uninstructed worldling might become disenchanted, might become dispassionate, and might be liberated.

But as for this which is called "mind," or "intellect," or "consciousness"—in that regard, the uninstructed worldling is not capable of becoming disenchanted, not capable of becoming dispassionate, and not capable of being liberated. Why is that?
For a long time, bhikkhus, this has been clung to, claimed as "mine," and adhered to by the uninstructed worldling:
"This is mine, this I am, this is my self.
Therefore, in regard to that, the uninstructed worldling is not capable of becoming disenchanted, not capable of becoming dispassionate, and not capable of being liberated.
“Monks, it would be better for an uninstructed worldling to regard this body composed of the four great elements as self rather than the mind. Why is that?
Monks, this body composed of the four great elements can be seen to remain for one year, or even for two years.”
Remaining for three years, remaining for four years, remaining for five years, remaining for ten years,
remaining for twenty years, remaining for thirty years,
remaining for forty years, remaining for fifty years, [or] even for a hundred years.
"Whether standing still or standing even more firmly,
monks, that which is called 'mind,' or 'intellect,' or 'consciousness,' arises as one thing and ceases as another, both by night and by day.
In this regard, monks, the well-taught noble disciple carefully and thoroughly attends to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) thus:"
‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.
Monks, in dependence on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—namely, the pleasant feeling arisen in dependence on the contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and subsides.
Monks, in dependence on contact to be experienced as painful, a painful feeling arises.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as painful, the corresponding feeling—namely, the painful feeling arisen in dependence on the contact to be experienced as painful—ceases and subsides.
“Monks, dependent on a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, there arises a feeling to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, whatever corresponding feeling to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant had arisen dependent on that contact ceases and subsides.
Just as, monks, from the friction and conjunction of two pieces of wood, heat is produced and fire is generated;”

Just as the heat produced from those same two pieces of wood ceases and subsides when they are separated and divided, even so, monks, dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding sensation—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and subsides... [and so on].
In dependence on a contact to be experienced as painful...
in dependence on a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, a feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant arises.

With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, whatever corresponding feeling—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose in dependence on that contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—ceases and subsides.

"Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with contact, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises:
'It is liberated. He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'"
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.63 (SN 12.63, PTS SN ii 97) 7. Mahāvagga
The Discourse on Meat from a Putrid Corpse.
At Sāvatthī...
"Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have come to be or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth."
Which four?
Edible food, whether gross or subtle; second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness.
These, monks, are the four foods for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
And how, monks, should edible food be regarded?
Suppose, monks, a husband and wife were to set out on a desert journey, taking with them a small amount of provisions.
They would have an only son, dear and beloved.
Then, monks, when the small amount of provisions those two husband and wife had while traveling through the wilderness was exhausted and used up,
and there remained a portion of the wilderness yet to be crossed,
it occurred to them, monks, that those two husband and wife:
"Our limited provisions for the journey have been exhausted and consumed.
Yet this remainder of the wilderness has not yet been crossed.

What if we were to kill this only son, who is dear and beloved to us, and prepare dried meat and broth? By eating our son’s flesh, we might cross this remainder of the wilderness; let us not all three perish."

Then, monks, those two parents, having slaughtered that only son—dear and beloved—having made him into dried meat and jerky, might cross the remainder of that wilderness while eating their son’s flesh.
They would eat their son’s flesh and beat their breasts, crying out:
“Where are you, our only son? Where are you, our only son?”
“What do you think, monks,
would they take food for sport, or take food for intoxication, or take food for beautification, or take food for embellishment?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Monks, would you not take food only for the purpose of crossing the desert?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, monks, I say that physical nutriment is to be regarded in this very manner.”
“Bhikkhus, when edible food is fully understood, lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood.
When lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood, there is no fetter by which a noble disciple might return again to this world.
And how, bhikkhus, is contact as nutriment to be regarded?
“Monks, it is just as if a hideless cow were to stand leaning against a wall: whatever creatures live in that wall would devour her.
If she were to stand leaning against a tree, whatever creatures live in that tree would devour her.
If she were to stand leaning against water, whatever creatures live in that water would devour her.”
If she were to stand relying on space, the creatures that rely on space would devour her.
For whatever she might stand relying upon, monks, the creatures that rely on that would devour her.
In the same way, monks, I say that the nutriment of contact is to be regarded.
“Bhikkhus, when the nutriment of contact is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood.
When the three feelings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further to be done for a noble disciple.
And how, bhikkhus, is the nutriment of mental volition to be seen?”
“Monks, suppose there were a charcoal pit more than a man’s height deep, filled with glowing coals, free from smoke.
Then a man might come along, desiring life, not wishing for death, desiring happiness and recoiling from suffering.
Two strong men, seizing him by both arms, would drag him toward that charcoal pit.”
Then, monks, that man’s intention would be far off, his aspiration far off, and his resolve far off.
Why is that? Because, monks, it occurs to that man thus:
‘I shall fall into this pit of glowing embers; on that account, I will meet death or suffering amounting to death.
In the same way, monks, I say that mental volition as nutriment is to be regarded.
When mental volition as nutriment is fully understood, monks, the three kinds of craving are fully understood.
"When the three kinds of craving have been fully understood, I say there is nothing further to be done for the noble disciple.
And how, bhikkhus, is the nutriment consciousness to be regarded?
Suppose, bhikkhus, they were to seize a bandit, a criminal, and bring him before the king, saying:"
‘Your Majesty, this is a thief, a criminal; inflict upon him whatever punishment you wish.
Then the king might say to him:
‘Go, sirs, strike this man with a hundred spears at the time of morning.’”
Suppose they were to strike him with a hundred spears in the morning.
Then, at midday, the king might ask:
"Hey, what has become of that man?"
‘In that very same way, Your Majesty, he is still alive.
Then the king would say to him:
‘Go, sirs, at the time of midday, strike that man with a hundred spears.’
Suppose they were to strike him with a hundred spears at midday.
Then, in the evening, the king might ask:
"Ho there! What is that man like?"
‘In the same way, Your Majesty, he is still alive.
Then the king might say to him:
‘Go, sirs, strike that man with a hundred spears in the evening.’”
Suppose they were to strike him with a hundred spears in the evening.
What do you think, monks,
would that man, being struck by three hundred spears throughout the day, experience pain and grief on that account?”
“Venerable sir, even if one were struck by a single spear, one would experience suffering and mental distress on that account;
what need is there to speak of being struck by three hundred spears?
“In the same way, monks, I say that the nutriment of consciousness is to be regarded.”

“Bhikkhus, when consciousness as nutriment is fully understood, name-and-form is fully understood. When name-and-form is fully understood, I say that for the noble disciple there is nothing further to be done.
Thus was the third [discourse]. Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.64 (SN 12.64, PTS SN ii 101).
7. Mahāvagga:
Atthirāgasutta.
At Sāvatthī he was staying.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
What are the four?
Edible food, whether gross or subtle; second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness.”
“Monks, these four nutriments are for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
If there is lust for physical nutriment, monks, if there is delight in it, if there is craving for it, consciousness becomes established there and grows.
Wherever consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form.”
Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations.
Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.
"Wherever there is future birth, aging, and death, that, monks, I say is accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by fear, and accompanied by despair.
Whether it be with contact as nutriment...
or with mental volition as nutriment..."
If, monks, there is lust for the nutriment consciousness, if there is delight, if there is craving, then consciousness becomes established there and grows.
Wherever consciousness becomes established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form.
Wherever there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of formations.
Wherever there is growth of formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
Wherever there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.
Wherever there is birth, aging, and death in the future, I say, monks, that it is accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by fear, and accompanied by despair.
“Just as, monks, a dyer or a painter, using dye or lac or turmeric or indigo or crimson,
might create on a well-polished plank or wall or canvas the form of a woman or a man,
complete in all its limbs and features;”
In the same way, monks, if there is lust for physical nutriment, if there is delight, if there is craving, consciousness becomes established there and grows.
Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form.
Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of formations.
Wherever there is the increase of volitional formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
Wherever there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.
Wherever there is birth, aging, and death in the future, I say, monks, that it is accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by fear, and accompanied by despair.
If, monks, there is lust for the nutriment of contact...
if, monks, there is lust for the nutriment of mental volition...
if, monks, there is lust for the nutriment of consciousness, there is delight, there is craving; therein consciousness becomes established and grows.
Wherever consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form.
Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations.
Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
Wherever there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.
Wherever there is birth, aging, and death in the future, I say, monks, that it is accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by fear, and accompanied by despair.
But if, monks, there is no lust for physical food, no delight, and no craving, then consciousness is not established there and does not grow.
Where consciousness is unestablished and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form.
Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations.
Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of renewed existence in the future.

Where there is no production of renewed existence in the future, there is no birth, aging, and death in the future. Where there is no birth, aging, and death in the future, I say, monks, that it is sorrowless, free from distress, and without despair. This is true if contact is the nutriment... [and so on]... ...if mental volition is the nutriment... [and so on]... ...if consciousness is the nutriment. Monks, when consciousness has ceased and does not arise again, there is no support for the production of renewed existence in the future. Where there is no production of renewed existence in the future, there is no birth, aging, and death in the future. Where there is no birth, aging, and death in the future, I say, monks, that it is sorrowless, free from distress, and without despair. This is how there comes to be the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This is what was said by the Blessed One, and thus I have heard it.

“Bhikkhus, if there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for the nutriment of mental volition… or for the nutriment of consciousness, then consciousness does not become established there and does not come to growth.
Where consciousness is not established and does not come to growth, there is no descent of name-and-form.”
Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations.
Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of renewed existence in the future.
Where there is no production of renewed existence in the future, there is no birth, aging, and death in the future.
“Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, that, monks, I call griefless, dustless, and free from despair.
Just as, monks, when the sun rises in the north, south, or east, a ray of light enters through a window-opening—where would it settle?
“On the western wall, Blessed One.”
“Bhikkhus, if there were no western wall, where would it be established?
“On the earth, Bhante.
“Bhikkhus, if there were no earth, where would it be established?”
“In water, Bhante.
“If there were no water, monks, where would it be established?
“It would be unestablished, Bhante.”
“In the same way, bhikkhus, if there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for the nutriment of physical food … [as before] … if there is no lust, no delight,
and no craving for the nutriment of contact … if there is no lust,
no delight, and no craving for the nutriment of mental volition …”
If, monks, there is no lust for the nutriment consciousness, no delight, and no craving, then consciousness does not become established there and does not come to growth.
Where consciousness is not established and does not come to growth, there is no descent of name-and-form.
Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of the formations.
“Where there is no growth of formations, there is no production of renewed existence in the future.
Where there is no production of renewed existence in the future, there is no birth, aging, and death in the future.
That which is without birth, aging, and death in the future, monks, I call sorrowless, free from distress, and without despair.”
The Fourth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.65 (SN 12.65, PTS SN ii 104) 7. Mahāvagga
The Discourse on the City. At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was dwelling there.
“Bhikkhus, before my full enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, this occurred to me:”
“Alas, this world has fallen into hardship; it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn.
Yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death.
When, indeed, will the escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be made known?”
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"When what exists does aging and death come to be? With what as condition does aging and death arise?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there was a breakthrough by means of wisdom in me:
‘When there is birth, aging-and-death comes to be; with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘What being present does birth come to be? …’ [and so on].
There is existence; there is clinging;
there is craving.
There is feeling … there is contact … there are the six sense bases …
“Name-and-form comes to be...
With what as condition does name-and-form come to be?
Then, bhikkhus, through careful attention, there arose in me the breakthrough by wisdom: [the realization that] with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be.
‘When consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Now, when what exists does consciousness come to be? By what condition is there consciousness?’”
“Through careful attention, bhikkhus, there arose in me a breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When name-and-form exists, consciousness comes to be; consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.
Then, bhikkhus, this occurred to me:”
This consciousness turns back from name-and-form; it does not go beyond it.
To this extent, one is born, or ages, or dies, or passes away, or reappears—that is to say, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises ...
[and so on] ... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
“‘The origin, the origin,’ monks, regarding these things unheard of by me before, there arose in me the eye, there arose knowledge, there arose wisdom, there arose true insight, there arose light.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘When what does not exist does aging-and-death not come to be?’”
“With the cessation of what, bhikkhus, does the cessation of aging and death come about?
Through careful attention, bhikkhus, there arose in me the breakthrough by wisdom:
“When birth is absent, aging and death do not come to be.”
‘With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘When what is absent does birth not come to be? … [as before] …”
Existence does not exist … clinging does not exist … craving does not exist …
Feeling does not exist … contact does not exist … the six sense bases do not exist …
“Name-and-form does not exist.
Through the cessation of what is there the cessation of name-and-form?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in me the realization by means of wisdom:
‘When consciousness does not exist, name-and-form does not come to be;
with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘When what is absent does consciousness not come to be?
Through the cessation of what does the cessation of consciousness occur?
Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in me the breakthrough by wisdom:
‘When name-and-form does not exist, consciousness does not come to be;
with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of consciousness.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
I have indeed realized this path to enlightenment, namely:
with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness;
with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.
With the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases;
with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact ...
[and so on] ... such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
“‘Cessation, cessation,’ monks, regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. Just as if, monks,
a man wandering through a forest or a jungle were to see an ancient path, an ancient road followed by people in the past, he would follow it.”
While walking along it, he might see an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, inhabited by people of old, endowed with parks, groves, and lotus ponds, possessing ramparts, and delightful.
Then, monks, that man would report to the king or a high minister of the king:
"Please, sir, may you know: while wandering in the forest and the woods, I saw an ancient road, an ancient path, traveled by people of old; I followed it."
‘As I was walking along, I saw an ancient city, an ancient royal capital, inhabited by people of old, endowed with parks, groves, and lotus ponds, possessing ramparts, and delightful.
Venerable sir, please have that city built.
Then, monks, that king or royal minister would have that city built.
At a later time, that city became prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and reached the height of growth and expansion.
In the same way, monks, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road, followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past.
And what, monks, is that ancient path, that ancient road, followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past?
This very Noble Eightfold Path—namely, right view ...
up to ... right concentration—is that ancient path, that ancient track, followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of old; that is the path I have followed.
Following that, I directly knew aging and death;
I directly knew the origin of aging and death;
I directly knew the cessation of aging and death.

I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death. Following that path, following it further, I directly knew birth... [and so on] ...up to: ...I directly knew volitional formations. Following that path, following it further, I directly knew ignorance. Having directly known this, I understood as it really is: "This is suffering"; I understood as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; I understood as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; I understood as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. I understood as it really is: "These are the taints"; I understood as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; I understood as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; I understood as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: "It is liberated. I directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This is the third true knowledge I attained in the third watch of the night; ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute. This is the third true knowledge. I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death. Following that path, following it further, I directly knew birth... [and so on] ...up to: ...I directly knew volitional formations. Following that path, following it further, I directly knew ignorance. Having directly known this, I understood as it really is: "This is suffering"; I understood as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; I understood as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; I understood as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. I understood as it really is: "These are the taints"; I understood as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; I understood as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; I understood as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: "It is liberated. I directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This is the fourth true knowledge I attained in the fourth watch of the night; ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose, darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute. This is the fourth true knowledge.
I directly knew existence...
I directly knew clinging...
I directly knew craving...
I directly knew feeling...
I directly knew contact...
I directly knew the six sense bases...
I directly knew name-and-form...
I directly knew consciousness.
I followed after it;
Following after that, I directly knew conditioned phenomena;
I directly knew the origin of conditioned phenomena;
I directly knew the cessation of conditioned phenomena.
I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
Having directly known it, I declared it to the bhikkhus, the bhikkhunīs, the laymen, and the laywomen.
This holy life, monks, has thus become successful, prosperous, widespread, popular, and extensive, well-proclaimed among gods and humans.”
The Fifth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.66 (SN 12.66, PTS SN ii 107) 7. Mahāvagga
The Discourse on Right Mindfulness.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, where there is a market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Do you, bhikkhus, examine the internal examination?
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I indeed contemplate the internal while contemplating.
“But how, monk, do you contemplate the internal while contemplating?
Then that monk gave his explanation.
"In the way that monk answered, he did not satisfy the Blessed One's mind.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
"Now is the time for this, Blessed One; now is the time for this, Sugata."
“Whatever the Blessed One might say regarding the intermediate summary, having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Therefore, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, monks, a monk, while reflecting, reflects on an internal reflection:
‘Whatever various and manifold kinds of suffering arise in the world, such as aging and death—’”

‘What is the source of this suffering? What is its origin? Of what nature is it? From what does it arise? When what exists do aging and death come to be? When what is absent do aging and death not come to be?
As he investigates, he understands thus:
‘This manifold, diverse suffering that arises in the world—aging and death—[what is its source...]’”

‘This suffering indeed has acquisition as its source, acquisition as its origin, is born of acquisition, and produced by acquisition; when there is acquisition, there is aging-and-death; when there is no acquisition, there is no aging-and-death.

Thus he understands aging-and-death, he understands the origin of aging-and-death, he understands the cessation of aging-and-death, and he understands the practice that leads to the cessation of aging-and-death which is in conformity with that.
And he practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma.
“Monks, this is called a monk who is practicing entirely for the right destruction of suffering and for the cessation of aging and death.
Then, further investigating, he investigates the intermediate investigation:

‘But what is the source of this acquisition (upadhi)? What is its origin? Of what nature is it? From what does it arise? When what exists does acquisition come to be? When what does not exist does acquisition not come to be?’”
Thus reflecting correctly, he understands:

"Acquisition has craving as its source, craving as its origin, craving as its birth, craving as its provenance; when there is craving, there is acquisition; when there is no craving, there is no acquisition.
He understands acquisition, he understands the origin of acquisition, he understands the cessation of acquisition, and he understands the practice that leads to the cessation of acquisition.
And he practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma.
This, monks, is called a monk who is practicing entirely for the right destruction of suffering, for the cessation of the acquisitions.
Then, further reflecting, he reflects upon an intermediate reflection:
‘But where does this craving arise when it arises, and where does it settle when it settles?
As he reflects, he understands thus:
‘In whatever is lovely and agreeable in the world, there this craving arises when it arises, and there it settles when it settles.’
And what in the world is lovely and pleasant?
The eye is lovely and pleasant in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
The ear is lovely and pleasant in the world … [and so on for the nose, tongue, body, and mind] … pe …
The nose is a lovely thing in the world, a pleasant thing in the world;
the tongue is a lovely thing in the world, a pleasant thing in the world;
the body is a lovely thing in the world, a pleasant thing in the world.
The mind is a lovely thing in the world, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, in the past have regarded that which is lovely and pleasant in the world as permanent, as happiness, as self, as health, and as security—
They increased craving;
those who increased craving increased acquisitions;
those who increased acquisitions increased suffering.

Those who increased suffering were not liberated from birth, aging, and death; they were not liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they were not liberated from suffering, I say.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, in the future time, shall regard that which is dear and pleasant in the world as permanent, as happiness, as self, and as health—
They will see from a state of security; they will see.
They will increase craving.
Those who increase craving will increase acquisitions.
Those who increase their acquisitions will increase their suffering.
Those who increase their suffering will not be liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they will not be liberated from suffering, I say.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins there are now, bhikkhus, who regard that which is dear and pleasant in the world as permanent, as happiness, as self, as health, and as security—
They increase craving.
Those who increase craving increase acquisitions.
Those who increase acquisitions increase suffering.
Those who increase suffering are not liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they are not liberated from suffering, I say.
Just as if, monks, there were a bronze cup of beverage endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of taste, but it were mixed with poison.
Then a man might come, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, weary, thirsty, and parched with thirst.
They would say to him:
"O man, here is a bronze vessel of drink for you, endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of taste."
"But it is mixed with poison.
If you wish, drink it.
While you are drinking it, it will indeed please you in its color, its fragrance, and its flavor; yet having drunk it, you will consequently meet death or suffer pain amounting to death."
If he were to drink that cup of beverage suddenly and without reflection, and did not give it up, he would on that account meet death or suffer pain amounting to death.
In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins in the past [regarded] what in the world is lovely... [and so forth].
In the future...
[and so on] ...at present, whatever in the world is dear and pleasant, those ascetics or brahmins who view it as permanent, as happiness, as self, as health, and as security, increase their craving.
Those who increase their craving increase their acquisitions.
Those who increase their acquisitions increase suffering.
Those who increase suffering are not liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they are not liberated from suffering, I say.
And as for those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who in the past... whatever in this world is of a pleasant nature—
Those who saw that which has a pleasant form as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self, as a disease, and as a danger,
abandoned craving.
Those who abandoned craving abandoned the acquisitions.
Those who have abandoned acquisitions have abandoned suffering.
Those who have abandoned suffering are fully released from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they are fully released from suffering, I say.
For whatever recluses or brahmins there may be in the future time, [who regard] that which in the world is lovely...
They will see that which has a pleasant form as impermanent, they will see it as suffering, they will see it as non-self,
they will see it as a disease, they will see it as a danger;
thus, they will abandon craving.
"Those who will abandon craving...
they, I say, will be liberated from suffering.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins there are now, bhikkhus, who see that which is pleasant and agreeable in the world as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self, as a disease, and as a danger..."
They abandon craving.
Those who abandon craving abandon acquisitions.
Those who abandon acquisitions abandon suffering.
Those who abandon suffering are liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are liberated from suffering, I say.
Just as if, monks, there were a bronze vessel of beverage endowed with beautiful color, fragrance, and flavor, yet it were mixed with poison.
Then a man might come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, thirsty, and parched with thirst.
They would say to him:
"Come, good man, here is a bronze vessel of drink for you, perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste."
"But it is mixed with poison.
If you wish, drink it.
While you are drinking it, it will indeed please you in its color, its fragrance, and its flavor; but having drunk it, you will consequently meet death or suffer pain amounting to death."
Then, monks, that man would think:
‘It is possible for me to allay this thirst for liquor with water, or to allay it with whey, or to allay it with salt water, or to allay it with sour gruel;
yet I would not drink that which would be for my long-term welfare and happiness.’
Thus, having reflected upon that vessel of drink, he would not drink it; he would relinquish it.
On account of that, he would not meet death or suffering equal to death.
In the same way, monks, whatever recluses or brahmins in the past [regarded] what is in the world...
Those who saw that which is pleasant and agreeable as impermanent, as suffering, as non-self,
as a disease, and as a danger,
abandoned craving.
Those who have abandoned craving have abandoned acquisitions.
Those who have abandoned acquisitions have abandoned suffering.
Those who have abandoned suffering are liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are liberated from suffering, I say.
"Whatever recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, in the future... or at present,
see whatever is of a pleasant nature and agreeable nature in the world as impermanent, see it as suffering, see it as non-self, see it as a disease, and see it as a danger,
they abandon craving."
“Those who abandon craving abandon acquisitions.
Those who abandon acquisitions abandon suffering.
Those who abandon suffering are liberated from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are liberated from suffering—so I say.”
Sixth. Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.67 (SN 12.67, PTS SN ii 112) 7. Mahāvagga
The Naḷakalāpī Sutta.
On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having exchanged courteous and memorable greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, is aging-and-death self-made, or is it made by another, or is it both self-made and made by another, or is it neither self-made nor made by another but has arisen fortuitously?"

“Friend Koṭṭhita, aging and death are not self-made; aging and death are not made by another; aging and death are not both self-made and made by another; nor is aging and death arisen fortuitously, being neither self-made nor made by another.
Rather, with birth as condition, there is aging and death.
“But friend Sāriputta, is birth self-made? Is birth made by another? Is birth both self-made and made by another? Or is birth arisen fortuitously, being neither self-made nor made by another?”
“Friend Koṭṭhika, birth is not self-made; birth is not made by another; birth is not both self-made and made by another; nor is birth arisen by chance, being neither self-made nor made by another.
Rather, with existence as condition, there is birth.
“But what, friend Sāriputta, is existence self-made? … [and so on] …”
clinging is self-made … craving is self-made … feeling is self-made …
“Is contact self-made?
Is the sixfold sense base self-made?
Is name-and-form self-made? Is name-and-form made by another? Is name-and-form both self-made and made by another? Or is name-and-form neither self-made nor made by another, but arisen fortuitously?”
“Friend Koṭṭhita, name-and-form is not self-made, nor is it made by another; name-and-form is not both self-made and made by another, nor is it without cause, arisen fortuitously.
Rather, with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.

“But, friend Sāriputta, is consciousness self-made, or is consciousness made by another, or is consciousness both self-made and made by another, or is consciousness without cause, arisen fortuitously?”

“Friend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is not self-made, nor is it made by another; consciousness is not both self-made and made by another, nor is it arisen fortuitously, being neither self-made nor made by another.
Rather, consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.
“We understand the Venerable Sāriputta’s statement just now exactly thus:”

“Friend Koṭṭhika, name-and-form is not made by oneself, nor is name-and-form made by another, nor is name-and-form made both by oneself and by another, nor has name-and-form arisen fortuitously, being made neither by oneself nor by another.
Rather, with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.
And this is precisely how we understand the statement of the Venerable Sāriputta.

“Friend Koṭṭhita, consciousness is not self-made, nor is consciousness made by another; consciousness is neither self-made nor made by another, nor has it arisen fortuitously without being made by anyone.
Rather, consciousness has name-and-form as its condition.
“But how, friend Sāriputta, should the meaning of this statement be understood?”
“In that case, friend, I will give you a simile.
For by means of a simile some wise people understand the meaning of what has been said.
Suppose, friend, two bundles of reeds were standing leaning against one another.”
In the same way, friends, with name-and-form as condition there is consciousness;
with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form;
with name-and-form as condition there are the six sense bases.
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises...
thus there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
If, friend, one were to pull one of those bundles of reeds, the other would fall down.
And if one were to pull up the other, the latter would fall down.
In the same way, friends, with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness;
with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form.
With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
“It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta!
It is marvelous, friend Sāriputta!
How well this has been spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta!”
And we rejoice in this statement of the Venerable Sāriputta by means of these thirty-six grounds:

"If, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with aging-and-death, for dispassion toward it, and for its cessation, he is fit to be called a 'bhikkhu who is a preacher of the Dhamma.

If, friends, a bhikkhu practices for the sake of disenchantment with aging-and-death, for dispassion toward it, and for its cessation, he is fit to be called a 'bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.'"

If, friend, a bhikkhu is liberated through disenchantment with, through the fading away of lust for, through the cessation of, and through non-clinging to aging-and-death, it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life. If he is so regarding birth … if he is so regarding existence … [it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life].
If there were no clinging...
if there were no craving...
if there were no feeling...
If there were no contact … if there were no six sense bases … if there were no name-and-form …

If, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disenchantment with consciousness, for the fading away of lust for it, and for its cessation— and likewise for volitional formations and for ignorance— then he is fit to be called a bhikkhu who is a speaker of the Dhamma.

“Friends, if a bhikkhu is practicing for the sake of disenchantment with ignorance, for its fading away, and for its cessation, he is fit to be called ‘a bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma.

Friends, if a bhikkhu, through disenchantment with ignorance, through its fading away and its cessation, is liberated by non-clinging, he is fit to be called ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.68 (SN 12.68, PTS SN ii 115) 7. Mahāvagga Kosambī Sutta: At Kosambī At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. There the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you would dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, this is the way for you to do so: abandon what is unwholesome; Ānanda, cultivate the wholesome; abandon what is blameworthy; Ānanda, cultivate what is blameless; finish with the whole round of defilements; Ānanda, be pure in all things. This, Ānanda, is the way for you to dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does one abandon what is unwholesome? How does one cultivate the wholesome? How does one abandon what is blameworthy? How does one cultivate what is blameless? How does one finish with the whole round of defilements? How does one become pure in all things? “Ānanda, when one has clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is the origination and the passing away of the six bases of contact, it is in this way that one abandons what is unwholesome; it is in this way that one cultivates the wholesome; it is in this way that one abandons what is blameworthy; it is in this way that one cultivates what is blameless; it is in this way that one finishes with the whole round of defilements; it is in this way that one becomes pure in all things. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, is there the origination and the passing away of the six bases of contact? How is it that, when one has clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is the origination and the passing away of the six bases of contact, it is in this way that one abandons what is unwholesome... and it is in this way that one becomes pure in all things? “Ānanda, the eye arises and the eye ceases; visible objects arise and visible objects cease; eye-consciousness arises and eye-consciousness ceases; eye-contact arises and eye-contact ceases; feeling arisen from eye-contact arises and feeling arisen from eye-contact ceases; perception arisen from eye-contact arises and perception arisen from eye-contact ceases; volition arisen from eye-contact arises and volition arisen from eye-contact ceases; craving arisen from eye-contact arises and craving arisen from eye-contact ceases. The ear arises and the ear ceases... The nose arises and the nose ceases... The tongue arises and the tongue ceases... The body arises and the body ceases... The mind arises and the mind ceases; mental phenomena arise and mental phenomena cease; mind-consciousness arises and mind-consciousness ceases; mind-contact arises and mind-contact ceases; feeling arisen from mind-contact arises and feeling arisen from mind-contact ceases; perception arisen from mind-contact arises and perception arisen from mind-contact ceases; volition arisen from mind-contact arises and volition arisen from mind-contact ceases; craving arisen from mind-contact arises and craving arisen from mind-contact ceases. It is in this way, Ānanda, that there is the origination and the passing away of the six bases of contact. It is in this way that, when one has clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is the origination and the passing away of the six bases of contact, it is in this way that one abandons what is unwholesome; it is in this way that one cultivates the wholesome; it is in this way that one abandons what is blameworthy; it is in this way that one cultivates what is blameless; it is in this way that one finishes with the whole round of defilements; it is in this way that one becomes pure in all things. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he departed. Then, not long after the Venerable Ānanda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a cowherd with eyes were to guard his cattle, leading them from one pasture to another, and those cattle would eat grass that is edible, drink water that is potable, and they would find a pleasant place to lie down. Would that cowherd gain fame for himself because of that? “Yes, venerable sir.

“In the same way, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu dwells with mindfulness as his herdsmen, leading his mind from one station to another, and that mind of his eats what is edible, drinks what is potable, and finds a pleasant place to lie down, would that bhikkhu gain fame for himself because of that? “Yes, venerable sir. “What, bhikkhus, is edible for the mind? What is potable for the mind? What is a pleasant place for the mind to lie down? Visible objects, bhikkhus, are edible for the mind; sounds are potable for the mind; mental phenomena are a pleasant place for the mind to lie down. Suppose, bhikkhus, a cowherd with eyes were to guard his cattle, leading them from one pasture to another, and those cattle would eat grass that is edible, drink water that is potable, and they would find a pleasant place to lie down. That cowherd would gain fame for himself because of that. So too, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu dwells with mindfulness as his herdsmen, leading his mind from one station to another, and that mind of his eats what is edible, drinks what is potable, and finds a pleasant place to lie down, that bhikkhu will gain fame for himself because of that. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu dwell with mindfulness as his herdsman, leading his mind from one station to another, so that his mind eats what is edible, drinks what is potable, and finds a pleasant place to lie down? “Ānanda, here a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in the mind... He dwells contemplating mind-objects in mind-objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu dwells with mindfulness as his herdsman, leading his mind from one station to another, so that his mind eats what is edible, drinks what is potable, and finds a pleasant place to lie down. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... mind-objects in mind-objects, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world? “Ānanda, here a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short.
