On one occasion the Venerable Musīla, the Venerable Paviṭṭha, the Venerable Nārada, and the Venerable Ānanda were staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then the Venerable Paviṭṭha said this to the Venerable Musīla:

“Friend Musīla, apart from faith, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from the acceptance of a view after pondering it, do you have personal knowledge for yourself:”
"‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be’?
"Apart from faith, friend Paviṭṭha, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this; I see this:
‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be.’"

“Friend Musīla, apart from faith, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after deliberation, does the Venerable Musīla have personal knowledge for himself:
‘With existence as condition, birth comes to be’ ...
‘With clinging as condition, existence comes to be’?”
With craving as condition, clinging arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises;
with contact as condition, feeling arises.
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
“‘With volitional formations as condition, consciousness’ … ‘with ignorance as condition, volitional formations’?

“Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this; I see this:”
“‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.
“Friend Musīla, apart from faith, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it,
do you have personal knowledge for yourself that ‘with the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death’?”

“Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from approval based on contemplation of views, I know this and I see this:
‘With the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death.

“Friend Musila, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from approval based on contemplation of views, does the Venerable Musila have a personal knowledge for himself?”

‘With the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth’ …pe… ‘with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence’ … ‘with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging’ …
With the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact.
With the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases...
with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form...
with the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness...
“With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
“Apart from faith, friend Paviṭṭha, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this and I see this:
‘With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.’”

“Friend Musīla, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, do you have a personal knowledge for yourself that ‘the cessation of existence is Nibbāna’?

“Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this; I see this:”
“The cessation of existence is Nibbāna.
“In that case, the venerable Musila is an arahant whose taints are destroyed?
When this was said, the venerable Musila remained silent.
Then the Venerable Nārada said this to the Venerable Paviṭṭha:
"It would be well, friend Paviṭṭha; I might receive this question.
Ask me this question."
“I shall answer this question for you.
“May the venerable Nārada receive this question.
I ask the venerable Nārada this question.”
"May the Venerable Nārada explain this question to me:
Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from approval based on views,
do you have a personal knowledge for yourself that ‘birth is the condition for aging and death’?"

“Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this and I see this:
‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, does the Venerable Nārada have this knowledge for himself?”
“With existence as condition, birth...
[and so on] ...with ignorance as condition, volitional formations”?

“Apart from faith, friend Paviṭṭha, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this; I see this:”
“‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from hearsay, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, do you have personal knowledge for yourself:
‘With the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death’?”
“Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this and I see this:
‘With the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, does the Venerable Nārada have personal knowledge for himself?”
“‘With the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth’ …pe… ‘with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations’?

“Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from hearsay, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this; I see this:”
“With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from approval, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after deliberation,
do you have personal knowledge for yourself that ‘the cessation of existence is Nibbāna’?”

“Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, and apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it, I know this and I see this:
‘The cessation of existence is Nibbāna.
“In that case, the Venerable Nārada is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?”
“Friend, ‘the cessation of existence is Nibbāna’—this has been well seen by me as it really is with correct wisdom; yet I am not an arahant whose taints are destroyed.
It is just as if, friend, there were a well on a desert road, but there were neither a rope nor a water-bucket therein.
Then a man might come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, exhausted, parched, and thirsty, and he might look down into that well.”
"He would indeed have the knowledge that it is water, yet he would not dwell having touched it with his body.
In the same way, friend, although 'the cessation of existence is Nibbāna' has been well seen as it really is with right wisdom, I am not yet an arahant whose taints are destroyed.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Paviṭṭha:
“Friend Paviṭṭha, what do you say to the Venerable Nārada when he speaks thus?
“I say nothing, friend Ānanda, to the Venerable Nārada other than what is wholesome and other than what is skillful.
The eighth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.69 (SN 12.69, PTS SN ii 118) 7. Mahāvagga Upayantisutta At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by what being present, does aging-and-death come to be? From the arising of what do aging-and-death arise? “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take recourse in the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would clear up the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Bhikkhus, when there is birth, by the presence of birth, aging-and-death comes to be. From the arising of birth, aging-and-death arises. When there is existence, by the presence of existence, birth comes to be... clinging... craving... feeling... contact... the six sense bases... name-and-form... consciousness... formations. When there are formations, by the presence of formations, consciousness comes to be. From the arising of formations, consciousness arises. Formations have ignorance as their condition; consciousness has formations as its condition; name-and-form has consciousness as its condition; the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition; contact has the six sense bases as its condition; feeling has contact as its condition; craving has feeling as its condition; clinging has craving as its condition; existence has clinging as its condition; birth has existence as its condition; aging-and-death has birth as its condition. “Thus, bhikkhus, from ignorance as a requisite condition come formations; from formations as a requisite condition comes consciousness; from consciousness as a requisite condition comes name-and-form; from name-and-form as a requisite condition come the six sense bases; from the six sense bases as a requisite condition comes contact; from contact as a requisite condition comes feeling; from feeling as a requisite condition comes craving; from craving as a requisite condition comes clinging; from clinging as a requisite condition comes existence; from existence as a requisite condition comes birth; from birth as a requisite condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. “Thus, bhikkhus, for one who has seen well with right wisdom according to reality as it is—‘In this way, from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formations; from the cessation of formations comes the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; from the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. This is the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One, and so I have heard it.
Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There, indeed... [pe]...
“Bhikkhus, when the great ocean rises, it causes the great rivers to rise; when the great rivers rise, they cause the small streams to rise;
when the small streams rise, they cause the large pools to rise; when the large pools rise, they cause the small pools to rise.
In the same way, bhikkhus, when ignorance rises, it causes volitional formations to rise; when volitional formations rise, they cause consciousness to rise.”
They cause [it] to approach: consciousness, approaching, causes name-and-form to approach; name-and-form, approaching, causes the six sense bases to approach;
the six sense bases, approaching, cause contact to approach; contact, approaching, causes feeling to approach;
feeling, approaching, causes craving to approach; craving, approaching, causes clinging to approach; clinging, approaching...
Existence leads toward birth; existence, as it proceeds, leads toward birth. Birth, as it proceeds, leads toward aging and death.
Just as, monks, the great ocean, as it recedes, causes the great rivers to recede; the great rivers, as they recede, cause the small streams to recede;
the small streams, as they recede, cause the large pools to recede; and the large pools, as they recede, cause the small pools to recede.
In the same way, monks, ignorance, when it departs, causes volitional formations to depart; volitional formations, when they depart, cause consciousness to depart;
consciousness, when it departs, causes name-and-form to depart; name-and-form, when it departs, causes the six sense bases to depart;
the six sense bases, when they depart, cause contact to depart; and contact, when it departs, causes feeling to depart.
“Feeling ceasing causes craving to cease; craving ceasing causes clinging to cease; clinging ceasing causes existence to cease;
existence ceasing causes birth to cease; birth ceasing causes aging-and-death to cease.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 12.70 7. Mahāvagga Susīma Paribbājaka Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. At that time, the wanderer Susīma had gone to the Wanderers’ Park. There he addressed the wanderers: “Friends, there is no other ascetic or brahmin who teaches a Dhamma so well-expounded as the ascetic Gotama does. For the ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma that is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. And yet, though the ascetic Gotama teaches such a Dhamma, he still declares: ‘My teaching is incomparable; my teaching is unsurpassed. Come now, friends, let us go to the ascetic Gotama and question him about this matter. If he is asked thus, he will answer accordingly. And whatever he says, we shall remember. When they had spoken thus, another wanderer said to the wanderer Susīma: “Enough, friend Susīma! Do not say that the ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma so well-expounded. Why? Because the ascetic Gotama is one who speaks in praise of himself, and it is not easy to find anyone who can criticize him. Come now, friend Susīma, let us go to the ascetic Gotama and question him about this matter. If he is asked thus, he will answer accordingly. And whatever he says, we shall remember. A second time and a third time, the wanderer Susīma spoke as before, and the other wanderer replied as before. Then the wanderer Susīma, together with a large company of wanderers, went to the Blessed One. When they had arrived, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the wanderer Susīma said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, there is no other ascetic or brahmin who teaches a Dhamma so well-expounded as the ascetic Gotama does. For Master Gotama teaches a Dhamma that is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. And yet, though Master Gotama teaches such a Dhamma, he still declares: ‘My teaching is incomparable; my teaching is unsurpassed. “Susīma, if others speak in praise of me, you should not approve of it, nor should you reject it. But rather, Susīma, you should examine it for yourself. And when you have examined it for yourself, if you find that it is so, then you may accept it. “Master Gotama, if others speak in dispraise of you, what should I do? “If others speak in dispraise of me, Susīma, you should not approve of it, nor should you reject it. But rather, Susīma, you should examine it for yourself. And when you have examined it for yourself, if you find that it is so, then you may accept it. “But, Master Gotama, how should one examine the Tathāgata? “Susīma, you should examine the Tathāgata in regard to his conduct and his teachings. In regard to conduct, you should examine whether the Tathāgata’s bodily actions are preceded by knowledge and followed by knowledge, whether his verbal actions are preceded by knowledge and followed by knowledge, and whether his mental actions are preceded by knowledge and followed by knowledge. In regard to teachings, you should examine whether the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “Master Gotama, how does one examine the Tathāgata in regard to his conduct? “Susīma, in regard to conduct, you should examine whether the Tathāgata abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence. You should examine whether he is pure in these respects. “Master Gotama, how does one examine the Tathāgata in regard to his teachings? “Susīma, in regard to teachings, you should examine whether the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “Master Gotama, how does one examine whether the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise? “Susīma, here a noble disciple hears: ‘The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.

He reflects: ‘I am subject to old age; I have not yet transcended old age. It would be good if I could attain final knowledge for myself while still young. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time the Blessed One was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and he received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The community of bhikkhus was honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, and revered, and it received gains of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, not respected, not esteemed, not venerated, and not revered, and they did not receive gains of robes, almsfood, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick.
Now at that time, the wanderer Susīma was residing in Rājagaha together with a large assembly of wanderers.
Then the assembly of the wanderer Susīma said this to the wanderer Susīma:
"Come, friend Susīma, lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama.
Having mastered the Dhamma, you may teach it to us."
“Having mastered that Dhamma, we shall teach it to householders.
In this way, we too will be honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and we will obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
“Very well, friend,” Susīma the wanderer replied to his own assembly, and he approached the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached him, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Susīma said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Friend Ānanda, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.
Then the Venerable Ānanda took the wanderer Susīma and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, [he stood to one side].
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this wanderer Susīma has said:
'Friend Ānanda, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.'"
“Therefore, Ānanda, let Susīma go forth.
And the wanderer Susīma received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.
Now at that time, a declaration of final knowledge had been made in the presence of the Blessed One by many bhikkhus.
“I understand: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Then the Venerable Susīma heard:
“It seems that many bhikkhus have declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One.”
“‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—thus we understand.
Then the Venerable Susīma approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he exchanged greetings with them.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Susīma said this to those bhikkhus:
“Is it true, friends, that in the presence of the Blessed One you have declared final knowledge, saying:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’?
“It is so, friend.”
“Furthermore, venerable sirs, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you exercise the various kinds of psychic power:
being one, you become many; being many, you become one; you appear and disappear;
you go unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, as if through space; and you dive in and out of the earth as if it were water?”
"Would you do as follows: walk on water just as on land; walk on unbroken water just as on earth;
travel through the air cross-legged just like a winged bird;
and even with your hand, touch and stroke these two, the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful, and exercise mastery with your body as far as the Brahma-world?"
“No, friend.

“But then, venerable sirs, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you with the divine ear-element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near?
“No, friend.”
“Furthermore, venerable sirs, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you understand the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing their minds with your own mind—
do you understand a mind affected by lust as ‘a mind affected by lust,’ and a mind free from lust as ‘a mind free from lust’?”
You understand a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred;
you understand a mind free from hatred as a mind free from hatred;
you understand a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion.
When the mind is free from delusion, you know, "The mind is free from delusion";
when the mind is contracted, you know, "The mind is contracted";
when the mind is scattered, you know, "The mind is scattered."
Or, when the mind is exalted, you understand, "The mind is exalted";
or when the mind is not exalted, you understand, "The mind is not exalted";
or when the mind is surpassable, you understand, "The mind is surpassable."
Understand an unsurpassed mind as "an unsurpassed mind";
understand a concentrated mind as "a concentrated mind";
understand an unconcentrated mind as "an unconcentrated mind."
“Do you know a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind,’ and an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind’?
“No, friend.”
“But, venerable sirs, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you recollect your manifold past lives,
that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births,
twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births?

For one birth, for a hundred births, for a thousand births, for a hundred thousand births, and for many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both contraction and expansion:
“In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance...”
‘Having such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, having such a limit to his lifespan, passing away from there, he has reappeared here’—
thus do you recollect your manifold past lives in all their modes and details?
“No indeed, friend.”
“But, venerable sirs, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
see beings passing away and being reborn— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—
and do you understand how beings fare according to their kamma, [saying]: ‘Indeed, these worthy beings, by bodily misconduct...’?”
They were possessed of misconduct in speech and possessed of misconduct in mind;

they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings were possessed of good conduct in body and possessed of good conduct in speech...
‘...endowed with good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view;
these, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, you see beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly—
“Do you understand beings—whether ugly or beautiful, fortunate or unfortunate—to be passing away according to their kamma?
“No indeed, friend.
“But when you know and see thus, do you dwell having personally realized with your own body those peaceful liberations that transcend the realm of form, the formless attainments?”
“No, friend. “In that case, venerable sirs, there is this explanation and yet the non-attainment of these states;
how is this for us, friend? “We are liberated by wisdom, friend Susīma.”
“Venerable sirs, I do not understand in detail the meaning of what you have said in brief.
It would be good if the venerable ones would explain it to me in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what you have said in brief.
“Whether you understand it, friend Susīma, or whether you do not understand it, we are nonetheless liberated by wisdom.”
Then the Venerable Susīma rose from his seat, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Susīma reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had had with those bhikkhus.
“First, Susīma, comes knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*); afterwards comes knowledge of Nibbāna,” said the Blessed One.
“Venerable sir, I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement that has been spoken in brief by the Blessed One.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would speak to me in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by the Blessed One.
“Whether you understand it, Susīma, or whether you do not understand it, first comes the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa), and afterwards comes the knowledge of Nibbāna.”
“What do you think, Susīma,
is form permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”—
“But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change— is it fitting to regard it thus:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“Is feeling permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Is perception permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
… “Are volitional formations permanent or impermanent?”
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?
“Suffering, venerable sir.”
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, Susīma, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form [should be regarded in this way].”
"This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever feeling there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all feelings are "not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
‘This is self’—thus should this be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom.
Whatever perceptions there are ...
whatever volitional formations, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle ... [all these should be seen as they actually are with correct wisdom].”
Whether inferior or superior, whether far or near—all formations (saṅkhārā) should be seen as they really are with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle—[all should be seen in the same way].
Whether inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom, exactly as it is, thus: "This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self.

Seeing thus, Susīma, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
“Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Susīma, do you see that ‘with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be’?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Do you see, Susīma, that ‘with existence as condition, birth comes to be’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Susīma, do you see that ‘with clinging as condition, there is existence’?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”— “Susīma, do you see that ‘with craving as condition, there is clinging’?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“With feeling as condition, craving arises...
with contact as condition, feeling arises...”
With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
“‘With volitional formations as condition, consciousness’ … ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations’: do you see this, Susīma?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Susīma, do you see that ‘with the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death’?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Susīma, do you see that ‘with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth’?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“With the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence… with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging…”
With the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact.
With the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases...
with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form...
with the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
“With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; do you see this, Susīma?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“But knowing and seeing thus, Susīma, do you exercise the various kinds of psychic power—being one, [you become many]...”
Having become many, you become one again; you appear and disappear; you pass through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains without being obstructed, just as if through space;
you dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; you walk upon water without breaking the surface as if on earth; and you travel cross-legged through the sky.
"Do you claim, Kāmase, that you are like a winged bird, such that you can touch and stroke with your hand even the moon and sun,
so powerful and majestic, and exercise mastery with your body as far as the Brahma-world?
"Certainly not, Bhante."
“But, Susīma, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, hear both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near?
“No, venerable sir.
“But, Susīma, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you, by encompassing the mind with your own mind, understand the minds of other beings, of other persons—”
"Do you know a mind affected by lust as a mind affected by lust...
[and so on] ...or do you know a liberated mind as a liberated mind?
"Certainly not, Bhante."
“But, Susīma, knowing and seeing thus, do you recollect your manifold past lives, such as one birth...
[and so on] ...thus with their aspects and particulars, do you recollect your manifold past lives?
“No, venerable sir.”

“But, Susīma, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, see beings passing away... [and so on] ...do you understand beings according to their kamma?
“No, venerable sir.
“But, Susīma, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you dwell having personally contacted with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form?”
“No, venerable sir.
“In that case, Susīma, this explanation and the non-attainment of these states—how is this so, Susīma?
Then the Venerable Susīma, prostrating his head at the Blessed One’s feet, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me—foolish as I was, deluded as I was, and unskilled as I was—that I went forth as a thief of the Dhamma in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline.
Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.

“Surely, Susīma, a transgression has overcome you—foolish as you were, deluded as you were, and unskilled as you were—that you went forth as a thief of the Dhamma in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline.”
“Susīma, it is just as if they were to seize a thief, a wrongdoer, and present him to the king, saying:
‘Your Majesty, this man is a thief, a wrongdoer; inflict upon him whatever punishment you wish.
Then the king would say to him:”

“Go, sirs! Bind this man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, shave his head, and lead him around from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the beat of a harsh-sounding drum.
Then, having led him out through the southern gate, cut off his head to the south of the city.”
Then the king’s men, having bound him with a strong rope by the arms behind his back,
shaved his head, and led him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the beat of a harsh-sounding drum,
would lead him out through the southern gate and cut off his head to the south of the city.
“What do you think, Susīma,
would that man experience suffering and mental distress on that account?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Susīma, whatever suffering and mental distress that man might experience on that account,
the going forth as a thief of the Dharma in a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya is a result even more painful and bitter than that,
and it leads to ruin. But since you, Susīma, see your transgression as a transgression and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.”

“This, Susīma, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one who sees a transgression as a transgression makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future.
The tenth.

The Discourse on Aging and Death.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One...

[said: "Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand aging-and-death, do not understand the origin of aging-and-death, do not understand the cessation of aging-and-death, and do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death,"
“Monks, those recluses or brahmins are not, in my view, recluses among recluses or brahmins among brahmins;
nor do those venerable ones, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life, enter and abide in the goal of the recluse or the goal of the brahmin.”
"Moreover, bhikkhus, whatever recluses or brahmins understand aging-and-death ... [and so on] ...
understand the way leading to it, those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, are among recluses reckoned as recluses and among brahmins reckoned as brahmins;
and these venerable ones, in this very life, have attained the goal of the recluse and the goal of the brahmin."
